title: What Is a Payment Gateway? How It Works, Types & Benefits
summary: Learn what a payment gateway is, how it works, its types, charges, security features, and how to choose the right payment gateway for your business.
body_text: Table of Contents Toggle Payment Gateway in 30 Seconds If you’re short on time, here’s a quick overview: A payment gateway enables businesses to accept online payments securely. It encrypts customer payment information before sending it for authorization. Supports multiple payment methods including UPI, credit cards, debit cards, wallets, net banking, EMI, and BNPL. Works with acquiring banks, card networks, and issuing banks to complete a transaction. Most Indian payment gateways charge between 1.6% and 3% per successful transaction. Features like high payment success rates, fast settlements, strong security, and developer-friendly APIs are key factors when choosing a payment gateway. What Is a Payment Gateway? A payment gateway is a secure technology that enables businesses to accept digital payments on their website, mobile app, or other online sales channels. It acts as the bridge between your customer, your business, and the banking network to process online transactions safely. Whenever a customer clicks “Pay Now”, the payment gateway securely encrypts the payment information, sends it to the relevant banks for authorization, and returns the transaction status usually within a few seconds. Without a payment gateway, businesses cannot securely accept online payments using: UPI Credit Cards Debit Cards Net Banking Digital Wallets EMI Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) International Cards Today’s payment gateways also help businesses improve checkout experience by offering features such as one-click payments , saved cards through tokenization, recurring payments, smart payment routing, fraud detection, and real-time payment status updates. Why Do Businesses Need a Payment Gateway? A payment gateway is useful for almost every online business that collects payments digitally. Common businesses using payment gateways include: Ecommerce websites D2C brands SaaS companies Online marketplaces Subscription businesses Educational platforms Healthcare providers Travel and hospitality businesses NGOs accepting donations Freelancers and consultants Mobile applications Digital service providers Regardless of business size, a payment gateway helps businesses collect payments securely while offering customers multiple payment options. Key Features of a Payment Gateway A modern payment gateway offers much more than payment collection. Some of its key capabilities include: Secure Payment Processing Payment gateways encrypt sensitive payment information before transmitting it to banks, reducing the risk of fraud and unauthorized access. Multiple Payment Methods Customers can pay using: UPI Credit Cards Debit Cards Net Banking Mobile Wallets EMI Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) International Cards Providing more payment choices often leads to higher checkout conversion rates. Faster Checkout Experience Features such as tokenization, saved cards, express checkout, and smart retries help customers complete purchases with fewer steps. Fraud Prevention Modern gateways use AI-powered fraud detection, risk scoring, velocity checks, device fingerprinting, and tokenization to identify suspicious transactions before they are processed. Easy Integration Most payment gateways provide APIs, SDKs, plugins, and no-code integrations for platforms like Shopify, WooCommerce, Magento, and custom websites. Real-Time Payment Tracking Businesses can monitor payment status, refunds, settlements, disputes, and transaction reports through a centralized dashboard. Example of a Payment Gateway Imagine you own an online clothing store. A customer purchases a jacket worth ₹2,000 and proceeds to checkout. They choose to pay using UPI. Here’s what happens behind the scenes: The customer scans the QR code or approves the UPI payment. The payment gateway encrypts the transaction details. The payment request is sent to the banking network for authorization. The customer’s bank verifies the account balance and approves the transaction. The payment gateway immediately notifies both the customer and the merchant that the payment was successful. The funds are settled into the merchant’s bank account according to the agreed settlement schedule. The entire process typically takes only a few seconds, even though multiple financial institutions are involved. Difference Between Payment Gateway and Payment Terminal Although both help businesses accept payments, they are designed for different environments. Feature Payment Gateway Payment Terminal Primary Use Online payments In-store payments Where It Works Websites, mobile apps, ecommerce stores Retail stores, restaurants, hotels, supermarkets Customer Payment Method UPI, Cards, Wallets, Net Banking, EMI Tap, Swipe or Insert Card Hardware Required No Yes (POS Device) Internet Required Yes Usually Yes Typical Users Ecommerce businesses, SaaS, marketplaces Physical retail businesses Customer Interaction Online checkout Physical checkout counter A payment gateway is designed for accepting payments online, while a payment terminal is used for face-to-face transactions in physical stores. Many businesses today use both to provide a unified payment experience across online and offline sales channels. Difference Between Payment Gateway and Payment Processor The terms payment gateway and payment processor are often used interchangeably, but they perform different roles in an online transaction. Think of it this way: The payment gateway securely collects and transmits payment information. The payment processor moves the payment request through the banking system and facilitates fund transfer. Feature Payment Gateway Payment Processor Primary Role Securely transmits payment information Processes and routes the transaction between banks Handles Customer Checkout Yes No Encrypts Payment Details Yes No Sends Authorization Request Yes Yes Transfers Funds No Yes Customer Interaction Visible during checkout Operates in the background Required for Online Payments Yes Yes A payment gateway focuses on security and payment authorization, while a payment processor focuses on moving funds between financial institutions. Both work together to complete every successful online payment. Players Involved in Online Payment Processing Every successful online payment involves multiple participants working together behind the scenes. Although the transaction is completed in just a few seconds, several systems communicate with one another to authorize, verify, and settle the payment securely. Understanding these players helps businesses troubleshoot payment failures and choose the right payment infrastructure. Player Role Customer Initiates the payment using UPI, card, wallet, net banking, or another payment method. Merchant The business selling products or services and accepting payments online. Payment Gateway Securely encrypts payment information, routes authorization requests, and returns the payment status to the merchant. Payment Processor Facilitates communication between the payment gateway, acquiring bank, card networks, and issuing bank. Acquiring Bank The merchant’s bank that receives authorized payments and credits the merchant account after settlement. Card Network Networks such as Visa, Mastercard, American Express, and RuPay that route card transactions between banks. Issuing Bank The customer’s bank that verifies available funds, performs fraud checks, and approves or declines the transaction. Example Suppose a customer purchases a laptop worth ₹50,000 from an online electronics store using a credit card. Here’s what happens: The customer submits payment details during checkout. The payment gateway encrypts the information. The acquiring bank forwards the request through Visa or Mastercard. The issuing bank checks available credit and performs fraud screening. The transaction is approved. The approval travels back through the same route. The customer receives an order confirmation. The merchant receives the payment according to the settlement schedule. Although multiple organizations are involved, this entire process usually takes only 2–5 seconds . How Does a Payment Gateway Work? A payment gateway acts as the secure communication bridge between the customer, merchant, and banking network. It ensures that payment information is transmitted safely while completing authorization within seconds. Here’s the complete payment workflow. Step 1: Customer Initiates Payment The customer selects a payment method, such as UPI, credit/debit card, net banking, wallet, or EMI, and enters the payment details at checkout. Step 2: Payment Details Are Secured The payment gateway encrypts the payment information and securely sends it for authorization. Modern gateways also use tokenization and fraud detection to protect sensitive data. Step 3: Payment Request Is Sent to the Bank The encrypted payment request is forwarded to the merchant’s acquiring bank through the payment processor. Step 4: Transaction Is Authorized The card network or UPI network routes the request to the customer’s issuing bank, which verifies the payment details, checks available funds, and approves or declines the transaction. Step 5: Response Is Returned The authorization result is sent back to the payment gateway, which instantly informs both the customer and the merchant whether the payment was successful. Step 6: Order Is Confirmed If the payment is approved, the customer sees a success message and the merchant can begin processing the order. If declined, the customer can retry using another payment method. Step 7: Funds Are Settled Once the transaction is authorized, the acquiring bank transfers the funds to the merchant’s account based on the payment gateway’s settlement cycle, such as Instant Settlement, T+1, or T+2. What Measures Do Payment Gateways Take to Protect Customer Information? Security is one of the primary reasons businesses use payment gateways instead of processing payment information themselves. Modern payment gateways employ multiple layers of protection to secure sensitive payment data throughout the transaction lifecycle. Some of the most common security measures include: End-to-end encryption Network tokenization PCI DSS compliance Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) Secure Socket Layer (SSL/TLS) encryption AI-powered fraud detection Device fingerprinting Risk scoring Velocity checks Real-time transaction monitoring These technologies help reduce fraud, protect customer information, and improve trust during online checkout. Security Features of Modern Payment Gateways in India When evaluating a payment gateway, businesses should look for the following security capabilities: PCI DSS Compliance for secure handling of cardholder data. Tokenization to replace sensitive card numbers with secure tokens. SSL/TLS Encryption to protect payment information during transmission. OTP and Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) for additional customer verification. AI-Based Fraud Detection to identify suspicious payment behavior. Real-Time Risk Monitoring to reduce fraudulent transactions. Role-Based Dashboard Access to improve operational security. Webhook Verification for secure communication between applications. Audit Logs for tracking payment activities and compliance. A secure payment gateway not only protects customer information but also reduces chargebacks, minimizes fraud losses, and helps businesses maintain customer trust. How Do I Know Which Payment Gateway Is Best for My Business? Choosing the right payment gateway isn’t just about the lowest transaction fee. A reliable payment gateway should offer high payment success rates, strong security, fast settlements, and an easy checkout experience to help maximize conversions. Here are the key factors to consider: 1. Supported Payment Methods When choosing a payment method, check that it supports multiple options, including UPI, credit and debit cards, smart cards, e-wallets, buy now, pay later, and EMI options to suit customer preferences. 2. Ease of Integration Businesses should choose a gateway that offers simple and quick integration. There are multiple ways to integrate, such as APIs, plugins, or hosted checkout pages, reducing technical complexity at the time of launch. Also, before going live, check if the payment integration is working fine in the sandbox environment provided by the payment gateway partner. 3. Transaction Success Rate Choose a payment gateway that is known to have higher payment success rates and negligible payment decline or abandonment issues. 4. Pricing and Settlement Cycles Choose a payment gateway that suits your affordability and has reasonable transaction fees. When onboarding a business, Cashfree Payments has the lowest charges at 1.6%, making sure pricing remains transparent and reasonable for the business. Therefore, choose a gateway that is known for faster settlement cycles and thereby allows businesses to manage cash flow efficiently. 5. Flexibility to handle finances As businesses grow, the payment gateway should be able to handle higher transaction volumes without performance or server issues. This helps in improving customer experience and trust in the business and the gateway. 6. Customer Support and Analysis When the customer and the merchant are easily able to access their transaction details, it makes management of finances easier and more transparent. Every merchant should be able to access their own customised dashboard where they can oversee every transaction report in detail. Tip: The best payment gateway is one that balances affordability, reliability, security, and a seamless checkout experience for your customers. Payment Gateway Charges & Pricing Most payment gateways charge a Transaction Discount Rate (TDR) – a percentage deducted from every successful transaction. Many providers in India also offer zero setup fees and no annual maintenance charges for standard accounts. Component What It Means Typical Range Transaction Discount Rate (TDR) Percentage charged per successful transaction 1.6%–3% Setup Fee One-time onboarding fee Usually ₹0 Annual/Monthly Fee Recurring platform fee Usually ₹0 GST Tax applied on gateway charges 18% on TDR Settlement Time Time taken to receive funds Instant, T+1, or T+2 For example, if your business processes ₹1,00,000 in payments in a month at a 2% TDR , the payment gateway fee would be approximately ₹2,000 , plus applicable GST. Some providers also offer introductory pricing for new merchants or custom pricing for businesses with higher transaction volumes. Before choosing a provider, compare transaction fees, settlement timelines, supported payment methods, and any additional charges for international payments, refunds, or chargebacks. Conclusion A payment gateway is an essential part of any online business. It securely processes digital payments, connects customers with banks, and enables businesses to accept payments through UPI, cards, wallets, net banking, EMI, and other popular payment methods. When choosing a payment gateway, look beyond transaction fees. Consider factors such as payment success rates, security, settlement speed, ease of integration, supported payment methods, and customer support. The right payment gateway can improve your checkout experience, increase successful transactions, and support your business as it grows. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What is a payment gateway? A payment gateway is a technology that enables businesses to securely accept online payments. It encrypts payment information, sends it to the relevant banks for authorization, and returns the transaction status to the merchant within seconds. How does a payment gateway work? A payment gateway securely captures payment details, encrypts the data, sends it to the acquiring bank for authorization, and returns the approval or decline status to the merchant. Once approved, the funds are settled into the merchant’s account according to the settlement cycle. How much does a payment gateway cost in India? Most payment gateways charge a Transaction Discount Rate (TDR) ranging from 1.6% to 3% per successful transaction. GST is applicable on these charges, and many providers offer zero setup and annual fees for standard accounts. Which businesses need a payment gateway? Any business accepting online payments can benefit from a payment gateway, including ecommerce stores, SaaS companies, marketplaces, educational platforms, healthcare providers, travel businesses, subscription services, and freelancers. Can I accept international payments through a payment gateway? Yes. Many payment gateways support international credit and debit cards, allowing businesses to accept payments from customers in multiple countries, subject to applicable regulations and merchant eligibility. What is payment gateway integration? Your need to integrate your website or app with your payment gateway to accept payments. Now, most leading providers offer detailed integration guides and SDKs. Moreover, they offer integration instructions in all major languages. Your payment gateway integration will depend on your type of integration (seamless or normal checkout) as well as your OS. Here are some links you might find useful. Web Integration Standard Checkout Seamless Basic Seamless Pro Mobile Integration Android SDK iOS SDK React Native SDK Version 2.0.0 React Native SDK Version 2.1.0 Flutter SDK Cordova SDK Android Support SDK: Xamarin Xamarin AndroidX SDK iOS SDK : Xamarin Xamarin Forms SDK Plugins Shopify WooCommerce Magento PrestaShop WHMCS CS-Cart OpenCart WordPress StoreHippo What is Payment Gateway vs Payment Processor vs Merchant Account? A payment gateway encrypts/tokenizes the payment details. It also communicates the payment info between acquiring bank and the merchant A payment processor communicates the payment details and responses between card networks and Issuing and Acquiring banks The merchant account is a business bank account. Therefore, the merchant receives the settlement from the acquiring bank here Related Read: Payment Gateway vs Merchant Account and Payment Gateway vs Payment Processor

title: Why Some Publisher Partnerships Grow and Others Stall
summary: In adtech, technology may open doors, but strong partnerships are what turn opportunity into lasting growth.
body_text: During a recent Voices of AdTech conversation , I was joined by Emily Brewer, Head of Business Development, CTV Supply at Teads, alongside my co-host Amy China Wire, VP of Digital Studios UK at Teads. While the discussion focused on Connected TV, one theme kept resurfacing throughout the conversation: partnerships. As CTV continues to grow across EMEA, publishers, advertisers, agencies, and technology providers are navigating an increasingly complex ecosystem. New opportunities are emerging, but so are new challenges. Success depends on more than technology. It depends on how effectively organizations work together. That observation felt particularly relevant because the same principle applies across much of adtech today. As ecosystems become more interconnected, growth is increasingly shaped by the quality of relationships behind the technology. CTV Is Growing Because Two Worlds Are Converging CTV sits at the intersection of two industries that historically operated very differently. Television has long offered advertisers scale, premium environments, and high-quality content. Digital advertising introduced targeting, measurement, flexibility, and performance visibility. CTV combines the strengths of both, creating new opportunities for advertisers, publishers, and technology partners alike. At the same time, it introduces complexity. Every market has different viewing habits, publisher landscapes, technology partners, and measurement standards. What works in the UK may not work in Germany. What succeeds in Spain may look entirely different in Italy. As Emily highlighted during our discussion, much of what makes CTV successful today is not the technology itself. It is the partnerships and execution behind it. Strong Partnership Teams Understand the Business Behind the Business One of the themes Emily returned to repeatedly was the importance of understanding what matters to a partner beyond the immediate commercial conversation. It is easy to assume partnerships are primarily about revenue. Revenue matters, but it rarely creates lasting relationships on its own. The strongest partnerships emerge when both sides understand the broader business context. What is the publisher trying to achieve? What challenges are standing in the way? Answering those questions requires a different mindset. Rather than approaching conversations with a predefined pitch, effective partnership teams invest time in understanding the environment their partners operate in. Emily described preparing for important negotiations by anticipating concerns, identifying potential sticking points, and involving the right experts early in the process. What stood out was how much of that preparation focused on creating clarity rather than persuasion. The objective was not simply to secure an agreement. It was to build a solution that would continue to make sense months later. Transactional partnerships focus on the opportunity in front of them. Strategic partnerships focus on creating value over time. Trust Is Not Soft. It Is Operational. Trust is often described as a relationship quality. In practice, it is built through operational consistency. Partners trust organizations that communicate clearly, deliver on commitments, and remain transparent when circumstances change. The more Emily spoke about trust, the less it sounded like an abstract concept and the more it sounded like a discipline. Partnerships begin to weaken when expectations and reality drift apart. A commitment made too casually can create months of frustration. An unclear roadmap can undermine confidence. A lack of follow-through can outweigh years of positive intent. This is especially important in CTV because of how interconnected the ecosystem has become. Publishers, advertisers, agencies, technology providers, and measurement partners all depend on one another. When one part of the chain struggles, the impact rarely stays isolated. Trust becomes a competitive advantage because it reduces friction. It helps teams solve problems faster, navigate uncertainty more effectively, and have difficult conversations when necessary. The Best Teams Balance Structure and Adaptability Another part of the conversation that resonated with me was Emily’s perspective on performance and goal setting. She emphasized the importance of having clear objectives while remaining flexible enough to adapt as conditions change. In fast-growing areas like CTV, priorities shift. Markets evolve. New opportunities emerge. Without structure, teams lose alignment. With too much structure, they lose agility. The strongest teams seem to operate between those extremes. They know where they are heading, but they are willing to adjust course when circumstances require it. That balance feels increasingly important across adtech. The organizations that adapt fastest are rarely the ones with the most detailed plans. They are often the ones with enough alignment to move together and enough flexibility to respond when conditions change. Partnerships Reflect the Teams Behind Them As the conversation progressed, it became clear that Emily was not only describing successful partnerships. She was describing successful teams. Every example she shared depended on people bringing different pieces of information together. Local market teams understood regional nuances. Commercial teams understood client priorities. Technical teams understood what was possible. Creative teams understood how ideas could come to life. Strong organizations benefit from bringing those perspectives together. Different experiences bring different insights into the room, helping teams identify opportunities, challenges, and solutions that might otherwise be missed. Partnerships improve when teams have a more complete picture of the businesses they support. The Part of AdTech We May Not Talk About Enough Adtech is understandably fascinated by technology. We spend a great deal of time discussing formats, measurement, identity, AI, and infrastructure. But listening to Emily and Amy discuss CTV was a reminder that technology is only part of the story. Technology may enable growth, but partnerships determine how much of that growth becomes reality. The organizations that succeed are not simply the ones with the best products. They are the ones that build trust, understand their partners’ business challenges, and consistently create value over time. The more I listened to Emily describe successful publisher relationships, the more I realized she was describing something broader than partnerships. She was describing the combination of leadership and teamwork that sits behind sustainable growth. Perhaps that is the part of adtech we do not talk about enough. Behind every successful partnership is a group of people working together to create value, solve problems, and build trust over time.

title: AIM recognizes Bill Toney with prestigious digital identification industry award
summary: MENTOR, Ohio — September 18, 2025 — Avery Dennison’s Bill Toney has been announced as the 2025 winner of the AIM Paul Bergé International Business Development Award.
body_text: AIM recognizes Bill Toney with prestigious digital identification industry award MENTOR, Ohio — September 18, 2025 — Avery Dennison’s Bill Toney has been announced as the 2025 winner of the AIM Paul Bergé International Business Development Award. The award recognizes Toney's extensive work in advancing automatic identification and data capture (AIDC) adoption and awareness, signaling his leadership, innovation and international influence in the AIDC space. Bill Toney receives the award from Mary Lou Bosco, CEO, AIM Global. For almost 30 years, Toney's global efforts have significantly expanded the reach and practical implementation of digital identification technologies. His visionary leadership has accelerated the adoption of RFID, barcode and connected product solutions across key industries such as retail, food, quick service restaurants and logistics, while inspiring collaboration and standardization across regions and technologies. “It’s an honor to be recognized with such a respected industry accolade,” says Toney, who is vice president of advanced technology, Solutions Group, Avery Dennison. “Helping people realize the benefits of automatic identification and data capture builds more connected and rewarding experiences both in business and society. It’s an incredibly exciting time and I look forward to driving further innovation of these technologies in the years ahead.” AIM is the global industry alliance for stakeholders of RFID, barcoding, smart devices and other AIDC technologies. The Paul Bergé Award recognizes the extensive international AIDC business development efforts spearheaded by Paul Bergé throughout his career. Mary Lou Bosco, CEO, AIM Global, adds: “Like Paul Bergé, Bill has worked across global borders and cultures to unite fragmented markets around shared technological goals. He has taken bold steps to localize global solutions, adjusting technologies to local infrastructure and regulatory needs, while maintaining alignment with international standards and driving ROI across applications. His ability to build trust, ensure client-centricity, align stakeholders and deliver measurable results make him an outstanding leader and a very worthy award winner.” Media contact Jack Gibson Global PR Manager jack.gibson@eu.averydennison.com About Avery Dennison Avery Dennison Corporation (NYSE: AVY) is a global materials science and digital identification solutions company. We are Making Possible™ products and solutions that help advance the industries we serve, providing branding and information solutions that optimize labor and supply chain efficiency, reduce waste, advance sustainability, circularity and transparency, and better connect brands and consumers. We design and develop labeling and functional materials, radio frequency identification (RFID) inlays and tags, software applications that connect the physical and digital, and offerings that enhance branded packaging and carry or display information that improves the customer experience. Serving industries worldwide — including home and personal care, apparel, general retail, e-commerce, logistics, food and grocery, pharmaceuticals and automotive — we employ approximately 35,000 employees in more than 50 countries. Our reported sales in 2024 were $8.8 billion. Learn more at www.averydennison.com . About AIM AIM is the trusted worldwide industry association for the automatic identification industry. For more than 50 years, AIM has provided unbiased information, educational resources and standards to providers and users of these technologies. AIM membership provides access to an insider’s perspective on trends and opportunities along with a voice in shaping the growth and future of the industry. Member benefits include education, advocacy, and community, as well as a role in creating industry standards through collaboration. title: A Field Guide to My Data Science Internship at Zepto
summary: 🎙️ The Observer’s Log: Entry #01 “We arrive at the bustling, hyper velocity habitat known as Zepto. Here, time is not measured in hours or…
body_text: A Field Guide to My Data Science Internship at Zepto Zepto Tech 5 min read · 6 days ago -- Press enter or click to view image in full size 🎙️ The Observer’s Log: Entry #01 “We arrive at the bustling, hyper velocity habitat known as Zepto. Here, time is not measured in hours or days, but in ten minute increments. Today, a new species enters the environment: The Data Science Intern. Notice how they cautiously approach their workstation, armed with Python notebooks and an eagerness to understand the complex mathematical rhythms of quick commerce.” When I joined Zepto as a Data Science Intern on the Pricing team, I knew I was stepping into one of India’s fastest moving tech ecosystems. But reading about quick commerce at scale and actually building for it are two entirely different beasts. Working alongside my manager, Deepak Dhankani, and my buddy, Abhijeet Anand, my mission for the season was clear: dive deep into the world of inventory based pricing and build models that could react to dynamic supply and demand in near real time. Here is a look into my journey navigating the engineering, operations, and culture that make Zepto tick. Phase 1: Observing the Physical Backbone (The First 48 Hours) 🎙️ The Observer’s Log: Entry #02 “Before the intern can manipulate the digital data streams, they must first understand the physical realm. To build models for the wild, one must step into the wild. And so, the migration to the Dark Stores begins.” My onboarding during the first two days was far from a standard presentation slideshow. We were immersed straight into the philosophy and physical reality of the company. We kicked things off with an interactive session with Co-founder Kaivalya Vohra (KV). What struck me most was his clarity and humility; he emphasized that fast experimentation and deep operational thinking are what truly power the company. We also sat down with CTO Nikhil Mittal, who broke down Zepto’s engineering philosophy: building systems that are fundamentally observable, scalable, and resilient . The theoretical architecture came to life when we visited Zepto’s Super Stores and Dark Stores. Standing inside a Dark Store is like watching a highly optimized relay race, watching inventory being stocked, orders picked, and riders dispatched; all in real time where every second is accounted for . Phase 2: No “Intern” Labels in the Wild 🎙️ The Observer’s Log: Entry #03 “In many corporate ecosystems, the intern is kept in protective captivity, working on simulated data and sandbox projects that never see the light of day. But at Zepto, the environment demands immediate integration. Survival means shipping to production.” One of the most refreshing aspects of my internship was that there was no artificial divide between “intern work” and “full time work.” From day one, I was entrusted with real ownership. Get Zepto Tech’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Remember me for faster sign in Working on inventory based pricing, I was tasked with developing a pricing model that optimizes inventory availability while ensuring alignment with Zepto’s Pricing strategy. Under the guidance of Amit, Deepak and Abhijeet, I went from ideation to deployment at lightning speed. Just two weeks into my internship, my model was deployed live on a pilot! To scale the model across Zepto’s massive footprint, I regularly sat in on strategy meetings with Product and Planning teams. Getting out of the data science silo taught me three core skills: Translating Business to Tech: I learned how to dissect business requirement, ask the right questions about constraints, and frame it into a concrete mathematical optimization and predictive modeling problem. Experimentation Design: Structured A/B tests in a hyper local delivery environment; selecting control vs. test dark stores, accounting for demand spillover, and defining statistical significance for real-time metrics. Shipping to Production: Connected the model directly to live dark store inventory and pricing streams using ETL pipelines. Phase 3: The Mega Scale of the Mother Hub 🎙️ The Observer’s Log: Entry #04 “We now venture into the epicenter of the supply chain: The Mother Hub. Here, the sheer volume of data we process on our screens manifests as towering aisles of physical goods moving in automated harmony.” Midway through the internship, our team took a field trip to a Zepto Mother Hub. If the Dark Stores are the sprinters of the ecosystem, the Mother Hub is the beating heart. Witnessing the warehouse automation in action, a facility efficiently processing millions of products was mind-blowing. But what made me proudest as a data scientist was seeing in-house AI initiatives running live on the ground. A standout moment was seeing OdinEye (Zepto’s scalable computer vision face authentication system for attendance) seamlessly processing personnel in real time. Seeing machine learning solve tangible operational friction at scale reaffirmed why we build the way we do. Press enter or click to view image in full size Phase 4: Pack Bonding 🎙️ The Observer’s Log: Entry #05 “Even the most industrious pack must engage in ritualistic play to maintain social cohesion. Notice how the hierarchy dissolves on the turf, replaced by friendly competition and adrenaline.” It wasn’t all algorithms, pilot testing, and deployment metrics. The Data Science team made sure we took time to unwind and bond as a squad. Our team outing was an absolute blast, featuring a high energy mix of football, go-karting, and an unforgettable game of laser tag. Moments like these, laughing, competing, and collaborating outside the office, made the team feel like a community. Press enter or click to view image in full size Evolution of a Data Scientist 🎙️ The Observer’s Log: Final Entry “ As the season concludes, we observe a transformed individual. The hesitation of day one is gone, replaced by the confidence of an engineer who has tested their hypotheses in the real world. The intern has successfully evolved.” Reflecting on my time at Zepto, I realise I’ve gained much more than just technical proficiency in pricing models and data pipelines. I’ve learned how to build with velocity, collaborate cross functionally with product and planning teams, and design data science models that generate business impact.

title: Kling 3.0 Omni Character Consistency Guide
summary: Keep one character across every Kling 3.0 Omni shot: Elements, Omni Reference, voice binding, and the Flick workflow to build the reference pack once.
body_text: Kling VIDEO 3.0 Omni treats everything you upload — images, video clips, elements, text, and audio — as one combined prompt. More importantly, it can lock the identity of each character or object independently across a scene. That makes Kling 3.0 one of the strongest AI video tools you can use today for character consistency. This guide explains Kling 3.0 Omni, Elements, reference images, image-to-video, start/end frames, voice binding, and the Flick workflow for keeping the same character across every shot. Quick answer: how do you keep a character consistent in Kling? The best way to keep the same character across Kling shots is to create a reusable Element from reference media, then reference that element in every generation. For a major recurring character, the strongest method is a short clean video clip of the character. For single shots, use image-to-video from a locked still, ideally with start and end frames. Question Answer Best consistency method Video Element from a 3–8s character clip Best still-image method Multi-image Element or Omni Reference Best single-shot method Image-to-video with start/end frames Max clip length Up to 15 seconds Audio Native audio, including multi-shot text-to-video References Up to 7 images, or 4 images/elements when combined with video input Video input One clip, 3–10s, up to 200MB, up to 2K Voice consistency Voice binding on Elements Best use Character-driven AI video, action shots, recurring cast, voice-linked characters {INSERT TOOL USE TO GENERATE WITH KLING 3.0 OMNI REF HERE} Cast your character in Kling Build the reference pack once. Keep the same face in every shot. Kling 3.0 Omni at a glance Spec Kling 3.0 Omni Max clip 15 seconds, up from 10 seconds in VIDEO O1 Resolution 1080p and 720p modes Audio Native audio, including multi-shot text-to-video Modes Text-to-video, image-to-video, start/end frames References Up to 7 images, or 4 images/elements when combined with a video input Video input One clip, 3–10s, ≤200MB, ≤2K Image specs ≥300px, ≤10MB, .jpg/.jpeg/.png Credits 1080p: 12/s with audio, 8/s without · 720p: 9/s with audio, 6/s without · +video input: 16/s at 1080p The important concept is Omni Reference . Instead of treating your prompt, character images, style images, and clips as separate steps, Kling 3.0 Omni reads them together. Images, videos, elements, and text all become part of the same generation context. What Kling Omni Reference means Kling Omni Reference is Kling's unified input system. You can provide text, reference images, elements, and sometimes video input, then direct the model to preserve specific people, objects, styles, or motion patterns. For character consistency, this matters because the model can separate: Who the character is. What the character is wearing. What the shot should look like. What the camera should do. What the character should say or sound like. Which objects should remain unchanged. That is much better than trying to encode a recurring character in text alone. The consistency toolbox: three methods, ranked Method 1 — Video Elements This is the strongest method for a recurring character. Upload a clean 3–8 second clip of your character and Kling builds a reusable Element from it. The Element becomes a cast member you can reference in later generations. If the character appears across many shots, this is the method to use. Use a video Element when: The character appears in multiple scenes. You need the same face across different shots. You need voice binding. The character has distinctive motion, posture, wardrobe, or physicality. You are building a sequence, not a one-off clip. The ideal element clip is simple: neutral motion, clean lighting, visible face, stable wardrobe, no distracting background, and no extreme camera movement. Method 2 — Multi-image Elements + Omni Reference Use this when you have stills, not a video clip. A strong multi-image reference set should include: Front-facing portrait. 3/4 view. Side profile. Full-body outfit. Wardrobe closeup. Prop closeup if the character carries something important. An approved production still if one exists. Do not upload seven near-identical portraits. The model needs different information: face, silhouette, outfit, angle, and key details. Method 3 — Image-to-video with start/end frames For a single shot, generate the exact still first, then animate it. This works because still-image generation gives you more control over identity, wardrobe, composition, and lighting before video motion begins. Start/end frames are useful when the blocking matters: the first frame pins where the shot starts, and the final frame gives Kling a target to move toward. Use start/end frames when: The shot has precise blocking. The character must end in a specific pose. You need a controlled camera move. You are matching a storyboard. You are chaining clips into a longer sequence. Build the character before you animate The cheapest place to solve character consistency is before video generation. Generate or upload a clean hero image. Pick the version of the character you actually want to reuse. Build a reference sheet. Create front, side, back, and 3/4 views if the character will appear across multiple angles. Lock wardrobe and props. Make sure clothing, accessories, and signature objects are visible in the references. Create a clean element clip. Animate a simple 3–8s shot with neutral motion. Use the same element every time. Do not rebuild the character from scratch for each shot. This is the same principle behind Flick's Character Reference workflow: anchor identity once, then use that identity across stills and video. Voice binding: the underused half Kling 3.0 Elements support voice binding. You can extract the voice from an uploaded clip, or attach a separate 5–30 second audio sample. Kling recommends clean background audio and moderate speaking pace. For dialogue scenes, this is a major upgrade. A face without a consistent voice is not fully a character — it is a lookalike. A character Element with bound voice can carry both identity and vocal continuity across generations. Use voice binding when: The character speaks in more than one shot. You need the same vocal identity across a scene. You are building an episodic character or recurring cast. You want dialogue to feel like it belongs to the same person, not a new TTS pass each time. A good voice sample should be: 5–30 seconds. Clean, with minimal background noise. Moderate in pace. Emotionally close to the intended performance. Recorded without music underneath. How to use Kling 3.0 on Flick Kling works best inside a broader filmmaking workflow: build the references, generate shots, compare takes, and cut everything together. Flick is useful because the canvas keeps your references, elements, prompts, outputs, and edit decisions in one place. To use Kling on a Flick canvas: Open a fresh canvas. Create a new Flick project and choose the aspect ratio: 16:9 for YouTube/film, 9:16 for vertical, or 1:1 for square social. Create or upload your character. Start with a clean character image. If the character recurs, build a front/side/back or three-view reference sheet. Use Character Reference. Lock the character in Flick before generating scene stills. This gives you controlled character images to feed into Kling. Generate the scene still. Create the exact shot composition you want: lighting, camera angle, background, wardrobe, and mood. Select the image and choose video. Click the image node and choose Generate Video , then pick Kling 3.0 from the video model picker (our picker also lists a Kling O3 variant). Pick Kling 3.0 / Kling Omni Reference. Use Kling when the shot needs strong motion, character control, or audio-aware generation. Attach references or Elements. Add the character Element, reference images, start frame, end frame, and audio/voice input when needed. Write a motion prompt. Let references carry identity. Use the prompt to describe action, camera, timing, sound, and constraints. Generate variations. Try different camera speeds, motion intensity, and prompt constraints. Save useful frames. Use strong first or final frames as references for the next shot. Cut and grade. Keep the full sequence on the Flick canvas so the shots feel like one scene. 🎬 The core Flick workflow is simple: build the reference pack once, cast the character in Kling, then reuse that same pack across Kling, Seedance, Veo, FLUX, or any future model. The pack outlives the model. Kling prompt template Use this structure: Reference @Element1 as [character name]'s identity, face, wardrobe, and voice. Use [start frame / reference image] for the scene composition. [Shot type / camera movement] of [character] in [setting]. [Character action over time]. [Environmental motion]. Audio: [dialogue, ambience, sound effects, music direction]. Constraints: preserve face, wardrobe, voice, and body proportions; no extra characters; no readable text. Example: Reference @Element1 as Mira's identity, face, black raincoat, short hair, and voice. Use the selected image as the start frame. Slow handheld push-in as Mira walks through a rain-soaked alley and looks over her shoulder near the end. Neon reflections ripple in puddles, steam rises from vents, and jacket fabric moves in the wind. Audio: wet footsteps, city ambience, distant traffic, no music. Preserve Mira's face, coat, hairstyle, and voice. No readable text, no extra characters. Prompt examples for Kling 3.0 Omni Recurring protagonist shot Reference @Element1 as the protagonist's identity, face, wardrobe, and voice. Medium tracking shot of the protagonist walking through a crowded night market. They push through hanging fabric, glance left, then stop under a flickering lantern. Steam rises from food stalls, crowds move around the camera, handheld documentary motion. Audio: footsteps, fabric brushing, crowd murmur, distant scooters, no music. Preserve the protagonist's face, red jacket, black backpack, and body proportions. No readable text. Voice-bound dialogue shot Reference @Element1 as the character's face, wardrobe, and bound voice. Close-up inside a parked car at night during heavy rain. The character looks down at a phone, breathes once, then says: "I found the address." Passing headlights move across their face, raindrops streak down the windshield. Audio: rain on glass, soft car interior hum, natural dialogue from the bound voice, no music. Preserve identity and voice. No readable phone text. Start/end frame precision shot Use Image 1 as the start frame and Image 2 as the end frame. Reference @Element1 for the character's identity and outfit. The character walks from the doorway to the center of the room, stops, and turns toward camera. Camera slowly dollies backward while warm window light grows brighter. Audio: soft footsteps on wood, room tone, no music. Preserve the character's face, costume, and final pose. No extra people. Action shot Reference @Element1 as the same fighter across the shot. Wide handheld action shot in a rain-soaked courtyard. The fighter runs forward, slides behind a stone pillar, then looks up as sparks fall behind them. Rain blows across the lens, cloth and hair move with the wind, camera shakes slightly with the sprint. Audio: rain, footfalls, cloth movement, distant metal impacts, no music. Preserve face, armor, and silhouette. No extra characters. Object consistency shot Reference @Element1 as the same antique camera object. Slow studio orbit around the camera on a reflective table. Light sweeps across the lens glass, dust particles float in the air, and the background stays minimal. Audio: quiet mechanical rotation, soft room tone, no music. Preserve the object's shape, lens, buttons, and proportions. No logos, no readable text. End-to-end workflow for a consistent Kling character Cast the character as stills. Generate the character until the identity, wardrobe, and silhouette are right. Create a reference sheet. Include front, side, back, 3/4, full-body, and detail shots. Generate a neutral element clip. Create a clean 3–8s video of the character with simple motion and good light. Bind the voice. Use the clip audio or attach a clean 5–30s voice sample. Generate scene stills. Build the actual shots with composition and lighting before animating. Animate with Kling. Reference the Element in every generation. Use start/end frames for precision. Pin the shot when blocking matters. Repeat wardrobe and lighting language. Keep recurring descriptors consistent across prompts. Review for drift. Check face, hands, voice, wardrobe, and prop continuity. Grade the sequence. Color consistency is part of character consistency. Troubleshooting Kling character drift Problem Likely cause Fix Face changes mid-shot Too much motion or weak reference Shorten the shot, use a stronger Element, add clearer face references Wardrobe mutates Outfit not visible enough Add full-body and detail references; repeat wardrobe language Voice changes Weak or inconsistent voice sample Use a cleaner 5–30s sample with stable pacing Extra people appear Prompt is too open Add "no extra characters" and simplify the scene Object changes shape Object not isolated clearly Create an object Element or add multiple angles Shot ignores action Prompt overloaded Let references carry identity; use prompt for action only Style shifts between shots No shared look reference Use a consistent style/lighting reference and grade afterward Long shot breaks down Too much happens in 15s Split into two shorter shots with start/end frames Kling vs other models for consistency Model Max clip References Voice/audio Available today Best for Kling 3.0 Omni 15s 7 images / video Elements Native audio + voice binding Yes Character consistency you can use now Seedance 2.5 30s 50 role-tagged references Co-generated audio Closed enterprise beta Long reference-heavy scenes FLUX 3 20s Not fully public Synchronized audio Early access Picture-and-sound generation Grok Imagine 1.5 15s Reference-to-video Not documented Live Fast image-to-video exploration Flick canvas Project-level Character Reference across models Audio in project workflow Live Managing the full film workflow The honest read: Seedance 2.5 has the strongest paper spec for reference volume, but it is not broadly available. Kling 3.0 Omni is the strongest character-consistency system you can actually generate with today. Best practices for Kling 3.0 Build the character as stills before video. Use a video Element for recurring characters. Use multi-image references for face, wardrobe, props, and silhouette. Bind a clean voice sample for dialogue characters. Keep element clips simple and well lit. Let references carry identity; let prompts direct action. Use start/end frames for precise blocking. Keep prompts short enough for the model to follow. Generate shorter clips when identity starts to drift. Grade all shots together before judging final consistency. Common mistakes Trying to make a recurring character from text alone. Use references or Elements. Uploading near-identical reference images. Give the model different angles and details. Changing wardrobe language every prompt. Consistency requires repetition. Using a noisy voice sample. Voice binding depends on clean audio. Asking for too much action in one shot. Split complex blocking into multiple clips. Ignoring color consistency. Same character, different grade still feels like drift. Rebuilding the character each scene. Reuse the same Element. Frequently Asked Questions How do I keep the same character across Kling shots? Create a character Element from a clean 3–8 second video clip, then reference that Element in every generation. For single shots, generate the character as a still first and animate with image-to-video or start/end frames. How many reference images does Kling 3.0 support? Kling 3.0 Omni supports up to 7 images, or up to 4 images/elements when combined with a video input. Images should be at least 300px, under 10MB, and in .jpg, .jpeg, or .png format. What is Kling Omni Reference? Kling Omni Reference is the unified input system in VIDEO 3.0 Omni. Images, video, Elements, and text are treated as prompts together, and the model can lock each referenced character or object independently. Can Kling keep a character's voice consistent? Yes. Elements support voice binding, either extracted from the uploaded clip or attached from a separate 5–30 second audio sample. This helps keep face and voice consistent together. Does Kling 3.0 generate audio? Yes. Kling 3.0 supports native audio, including multi-shot text-to-video. Audio generations cost more credits than silent clips. How long can Kling 3.0 videos be? Up to 15 seconds per generation. Should I use Kling or Seedance for character consistency? Use Kling 3.0 when you need a strong consistency workflow available today. Seedance 2.5 has a stronger reference spec on paper, but it is still gated. Use Flick to keep the same reference pack ready for both. Can I use Kling on Flick? Yes. Use Flick to build the character reference pack, generate stills, animate with Kling, compare with other models, and cut the final sequence on one canvas. title: 15 Best Mya Chatbot Alternatives for 2026
summary: Compare 15 AI recruiting assistants replacing Mya Chatbot. See screening depth, fraud detection, ATS integration, and pricing to find your best fit.
body_text: Key Takeaways If you're replacing Mya Chatbot for 2026, prioritize tools that combine deeper screening, real-time fraud protection, and bi-directional ATS automation—otherwise you'll keep bleeding hours on manual handoffs while AI-generated candidates slip through. Mya is strong at conversational engagement and scheduling, but weaker on screening depth, integrity checks, and workflow orchestration. Leading alternatives (notably Alex and Mokka) focus on richer profiles, verification, and automated ATS updates to reduce recruiter workload. The comparison and scoring framework below help match a tool to your biggest constraint: fraud risk, signal quality, candidate completion, or ATS friction. Recruiters lose hours chasing no-shows and filtering unqualified applicants, while AI-generated résumés slip through unchecked and fragmented point solutions create endless manual handoffs. Mya Chatbot built its reputation on high-volume, low-friction engagement for frontline roles — but it lacks the screening depth, fraud detection, and ATS automation that modern hiring demands. As AI-assisted resume fraud climbs 30–50% and hiring teams face pressure to do more with less, that gap is becoming impossible to ignore. TA leaders and recruiting operations managers evaluating their 2026 tech stacks need solutions that go further: richer candidate profiles, real-time fraud detection, and bi-directional ATS sync — without adding headcount. What follows is a rigorous breakdown of 15 alternatives, scored on the dimensions that matter most. Here's what's covered: Why Mya's conversational strengths leave critical gaps against rising fraud threats The screening, verification, and workflow capabilities modern tools deliver — including real-time identity verification that stops AI-assisted answers before they reach a hiring manager A side-by-side comparison of 15 platforms on screening depth, identity integrity, and ATS orchestration A scoring framework to match each alternative to your specific hiring challenges Why Hiring Teams Are Looking Beyond Mya Chatbot Mya Chatbot earned its place in the market through effective conversational screening — engaging candidates via SMS, web chat, and messaging apps to handle early qualification, interview scheduling, and basic ATS integration. For frontline, high-volume roles, that was enough. It's no longer enough. Enterprise hiring teams now face two converging pressures. First, AI screening tools reduce time-to-hire by 40–70%, raising the bar for what automation should deliver. Second, AI-generated applications and proxy test-takers have become sophisticated enough to sail past basic natural language processing checks undetected. Mya's surface-level Q&A was never designed to catch them. The gaps show up across three dimensions. On screening depth, platforms like Mokka conduct comprehensive pre-screening interviews that collect accomplishment examples and measurable outcomes — producing candidate profiles that go well beyond what resume parsing or simple qualification questions can surface. On fraud protection, Alex Verify's real-time behavioral anomaly detection and deepfake identification address threats that Mya's basic checks cannot mitigate. And on workflow integration, tools like Alex Coordinator's bi-directional ATS sync automate candidate status updates across more than 33 platforms, eliminating the manual handoffs that cost recruiting teams hours every week. Assessment depth is another fault line. Mya handles scheduling competently, but it offers nothing comparable to HireVue's AI-driven asynchronous video interviews or TestGorilla's library of over 350 customizable skills tests — capabilities that give hiring managers substantively richer signals before a single human interview takes place. At-a-Glance Comparison Table: 15 AI Recruiting Assistants The table below offers a quick-reference overview of 15 alternatives, focusing on the dimensions most relevant to recruiting leaders evaluating replacements. Capabilities reflect what was explicitly documented in 2026 research sources; tools marked "Data not available" appear in industry tool lists but lacked detailed specifications in source materials. custom enterprise Mokka Profile enrichment beyond resumes with integrity verification Comprehensive pre-screening interviews with multi-source verification Deep ATS integration for seamless data flow Seat-based pricing for predictability Recruiterflow Data not available Data not available Data not available Data not available Fetcher Data not available Data not available Data not available Data not available Arya Data not available Data not available Data not available Data not available hireEZ AI sourcing with automated multi-step outreach Proactive pipeline generation beyond LinkedIn Data not available Data not available SeekOut AI-driven talent sourcing and rediscovery Large-graph AI search scanning 750M+ profiles Pushes screened profiles to Greenhouse and Lever Data not available TurboHire Data not available Data not available Data not available Data not available Eightfold.ai Deep skill/role matching with predictive analytics Bulk automation screens, schedules, and matches at scale Full ATS integration for recruiting and talent intelligence Data not available Paradox (Olivia) Conversation-oriented automation for basic Q&A and scheduling SMS-first engagement for high-volume frontline hiring Data not available Enterprise pricing typically $1,500–2,500/month base HireVue AI-driven asynchronous video interviews with behavioral analysis Uses AI to evaluate facial expressions and tone Integrates with Greenhouse and Workday Enterprise pricing typically starts $35K/year Sense Data not available Data not available Data not available Data not available Bullhorn (Amplify) Data not available Data not available Data not available Data not available SparkHire Data not available Data not available Data not available Data not available NoonAI Data not available Data not available Data not available Data not available How We Scored Each Tool Replacing Mya effectively means evaluating alternatives against the specific gaps it leaves behind. Four criteria drove the scoring here, each grounded in verified research. Screening Quality & Integrity goes beyond basic Q&A to assess how deeply a tool probes candidate qualifications and how robustly it detects fraud. Mokka's built-in integrity checks and profile inconsistency detection set a high bar for verification, while Alex Verify's real-time identity confirmation and AI-assisted answer detection address the fraud vectors that simpler tools miss entirely. Candidate Experience determines whether applicants actually complete the screening process. A poor experience at this stage costs enterprises thousands of missed applicants. Alex's 92% five-star candidate rating reflects its conversational, human-feeling interview design, while Mokka's asynchronous flexibility consistently drives high completion rates in high-volume scenarios. ATS and Workflow Integration separates tools that fit cleanly into existing operations from those that create new silos. Mokka's deep ATS connectivity avoids tool bloat, while Alex Coordinator's bi-directional sync across 33+ platforms means candidate statuses update automatically — no manual intervention required. Pricing and Scalability determines whether a solution can grow with your organization without becoming cost-prohibitive. Mokka's seat-based model provides per-recruiter predictability regardless of interview volume; Alex's annual contracts, starting at $36K, bundle enterprise-grade capabilities that would otherwise require significant additional headcount. One important caveat: scoring is limited to features documented in the available research. Many alternatives have not published detailed 2026 specifications, so vendor demonstrations and proof-of-concept pilots will be essential for a complete assessment. Screening Quality & Integrity Checks Traditional chatbots like Mya handle basic qualification questions competently, but they miss two increasingly critical needs: capturing evidence beyond self-reported answers, and detecting the sophisticated AI-assisted fraud that has become commonplace by 2026. Purpose-built platforms approach both problems very differently. Alex AI Recruiting Platform Alex AI Interviews conducts interactive two-way conversations with contextual follow-ups, incorporating technical assessments in languages like Python and JavaScript with role-specific fine-tuning. Available 24/7 across 26+ languages, the platform generates structured scoring on a 100-point scale for every interview. Alex Verify layers on top of this in real time, combining eye tracking, voice analysis, behavioral analytics, deepfake detection, and multi-signal monitoring to achieve a 98% detection rate for AI-assisted answers and 100% identity verification. At scale, the system can conduct over 5,000 conversational interviews daily — a capacity no human recruiting team can match. Mokka Mokka's pre-screening interviews collect accomplishment examples and measurable outcomes immediately post-application, building candidate profiles that go well beyond what resume parsing captures. Its Profile and Answer Integrity Analytics then cross-check those responses against resumes, LinkedIn, and third-party data sources, flagging AI-generated applications and factual inconsistencies before they reach a recruiter's desk. The result is verifiable, metrics-backed evidence of candidate quality rather than self-reported claims. Other Tools Several other platforms contribute meaningfully to this space. HireVue uses AI-driven asynchronous video interviews with behavioral analysis, game-based cognitive assessments, and predictive analytics dashboards. TestGorilla offers a library of over 350 customizable tests, with options to customize assessments and built-in anti-cheating measures. Mercer provides automated assessment proctoring with candidate authentication built in. For the remaining platforms — Recruiterflow, Fetcher, Arya, TurboHire, Sense, Bullhorn Amplify, SparkHire, and NoonAI — the available research contains no specific screening-depth specifications. Organizations evaluating these tools should request demos with a direct focus on fraud detection methodology and assessment rigor. Candidate Experience & Completion Rates Even the most sophisticated screening engine fails if candidates drop off before completing it. In high-volume hiring, drop-off isn't a minor inconvenience — it's thousands of missed applicants and a distorted talent pool. This is where the design philosophy behind a platform becomes as important as its feature set. Alex addresses this with a 92% five-star candidate satisfaction rating , driven by low-latency voice, high-quality transcription, and adaptive questioning that closely mimics real conversation. The 24/7 availability across native languages ensures no candidate is left behind by scheduling constraints or language barriers. Equally important, anonymous scoring — where names and demographic identifiers are stripped from evaluations — reduces hiring bias by 40% while audit trails document every decision for compliance purposes. Clients like Allen Recruitment have described the platform as a "game changer" for ensuring every interested candidate receives genuine consideration. Mokka takes a complementary approach. Its asynchronous flexibility lets candidates complete detailed pre-screenings on their own schedule, which is particularly valuable in high-volume scenarios where real-time availability varies widely. The structured format drives consistently high completion rates without sacrificing the depth needed to surface genuine qualification signals. For the remaining alternatives, the available research does not include candidate satisfaction data or completion rate benchmarks. During vendor evaluations, requesting NPS scores and completion rate data should be a standard part of the process. ATS Integration & Workflow Automation A powerful screening engine that lives outside your ATS is, in practice, just another source of manual work. Data silos, status update delays, and workflow friction cost recruiting teams hours every week and quietly erode data quality over time. Deep, bi-directional connectivity isn't a nice-to-have — it's the baseline worth demanding from any modern platform. Leading tools achieve this through REST APIs for reads and writes, webhooks for real-time event triggers, and SSO/SCIM for permission management. When your ATS fires an event — a candidate advancing a stage, a status change, a new application — a properly integrated platform responds automatically, keeping records synchronized without human intervention. Alex Coordinator syncs bi-directionally with more than 33 ATS platforms, including Workday, Greenhouse, and Lever, automatically updating candidate statuses as interviews progress. Mokka's deep ATS integration is similarly designed to eliminate tool bloat, pushing enriched profile data directly into existing workflows rather than requiring recruiters to toggle between systems. SeekOut lets users export selected candidate profiles from SeekOut into Greenhouse and Lever via manual export actions, and HireVue maintains an established integration with Greenhouse that can send candidates to HireVue assessments and return status updates into Greenhouse; HireVue's Workday integration depth is not specified in the cited documentation. For tools where integration specifications aren't publicly documented, sandbox testing during the evaluation process is the most reliable way to verify real-world connectivity before signing a contract. Pricing & Scalability Cost structures matter as much as capabilities when evaluating long-term fit. AI recruiting tool pricing ranges from as low as $0.99 per interview to over $100,000 annually, depending on the model and organizational scale — so understanding what you're buying at each tier is essential. Mokka's seat-based pricing stabilizes per-recruiter costs regardless of interview volume, making it predictable for teams with fluctuating or seasonal hiring cycles. This model typically falls within the $15–55/user/month range, as seen across comparable platforms like Manatal. Alex AI prices its platform through annual contracts starting at $36K for staffing firms , with custom enterprise arrangements for larger organizations. That positioning reflects the premium capabilities on offer — and when measured against the average recruiter salary of $60–80K annually, a platform capable of conducting 5,000+ interviews per day represents a substantial efficiency return. More broadly, budget-friendly SaaS tools start around $15/user/month, mid-market options like Workable run approximately $299/month, and enterprise solutions range from $30,000 to $100,000+ per year. Pricing transparency varies considerably across the market: some vendors publish structured tiers, others require a sales conversation before sharing numbers. When comparing options, factor in implementation fees and potential annual increases alongside the headline price — the total cost of ownership can diverge significantly from the initial quote. Annual contracts from $36K. Ideal for enterprise fraud protection and staffing firm scalability. Mokka : Delivers comprehensive pre-screening interviews that enrich candidate profiles beyond resumes, with built-in integrity analytics cross-checking responses against LinkedIn and third-party data to flag AI-generated applications. Seat-based pricing for cost predictability. Ideal for high-volume hiring requiring verification at scale. HireVue : Specializes in AI-driven asynchronous video interviews with behavioral analysis, game-based assessments measuring cognitive ability, and predictive analytics dashboards forecasting performance and retention. Integrates with Greenhouse and Workday. Ideal for sales and leadership roles requiring verbal skill assessment. Enterprise pricing typically starts at $35K/year. SeekOut : Excels in AI-driven talent sourcing and rediscovery via large-graph AI search scanning 750M+ profiles across 45+ platforms, with ATS and CRM integrations pushing screened profiles to Greenhouse and Lever without manual exports. Ideal for passive talent sourcing and diversity pipeline building. Eightfold.ai : Enterprise platform leveraging deep skill and role matching with predictive analytics for performance, loyalty, and retention forecasting. Bulk automation screens, schedules, and matches at scale with full ATS integration. Ideal for Fortune 500 companies requiring workforce intelligence beyond recruiting. Paradox (Olivia) : Conversational AI assistant focused on SMS-first engagement for high-volume frontline hiring, automating scheduling and basic Q&A to reduce no-shows. Similar in positioning to Mya with a mobile-first approach. Ideal for retail, hospitality, and hourly roles. Enterprise pricing typically runs $1,500–2,500/month base. TestGorilla : Offers science-backed skills testing with 350+ customizable assessments covering cognitive, behavioral, and technical competencies, plus anti-cheating proctoring that tracks behavior and screen activity, and AI auto-scoring for video responses. Ideal for technical and graduate hiring requiring verifiable skill evidence. hireEZ : AI sourcing with automated multi-step outreach from vast candidate indexes, semantic resume ranking, and proactive pipeline generation beyond LinkedIn. Focused on early-stage discovery and engagement. Ideal for recruiting teams building pipelines before active applications arrive. Recruiterflow : Listed in 2026 AI sourcing tool evaluations but available research contains no feature, pricing, or integration specifics. Evaluation should probe screening methodology, candidate experience metrics, and integration depth. Vendor evaluation should focus on fraud detection features and ATS connectivity. Request documentation on screening quality and workflow automation during vendor selection. Sense : Referenced in recruiting assistant evaluations but available research lacks specifications. Evaluation should focus on differentiation from basic chatbots and integration depth. Bullhorn (Amplify) : Widely described in staffing technology and vendor materials with detailed capabilities. Particularly relevant for staffing firms already on Bullhorn ATS — request integration depth information upfront. SparkHire : Described in multiple video interviewing tool lists, and available research provides detailed specifications of its capabilities. NoonAI : Listed in AI assistant comparisons, although only a limited number of the sources used in the research document NoonAI's specific recruiting features. Request details on screening methodology and candidate experience during vendor evaluation. Which Alternative Fits Your Use-Case? The right platform depends entirely on where your current process breaks down. Here's a practical framework for matching your primary challenge to the tools best equipped to solve it. Need enterprise-grade fraud protection : Opt for Alex AI Recruiting Platform . Its real-time identity verification and 98% AI-answer detection rate, combined with a 92% candidate satisfaction rating, deliver robust fraud prevention without degrading the applicant experience. Require predictable per-seat pricing with resume enrichment : Choose Mokka . Its seat-based model scales cleanly with team size and produces verified, metrics-backed candidate profiles that go well beyond what standard resume parsing captures. Prioritize video-based behavioral assessment : Select HireVue . AI-driven asynchronous video interviews with behavioral analysis and predictive dashboards make it the strongest option for roles where verbal communication is central to performance. Focus on technical skills verification : TestGorilla is the most rigorous choice. With 350+ customizable tests and anti-cheating proctoring, it produces evidence-based screening results well-suited to engineering and technical hiring. Building passive talent pipelines : Look to SeekOut or hireEZ . Both platforms excel at sourcing and outreach beyond active applicants, keeping pipelines full ahead of active demand. For Recruiterflow, Fetcher, Arya, TurboHire, Sense, Bullhorn Amplify, SparkHire, and NoonAI, the absence of detailed research data means proof-of-concept pilots are the most reliable path to assessing screening quality, fraud protection, and integration depth before committing. FAQ How does your pricing model work—per interview, per user, or a flat fee? Pricing varies by vendor. For example, Mokka uses seat-based pricing for predictable cost per recruiter, while Alex is sold via annual contracts (starting at $36K for staffing firms) with custom enterprise pricing. When comparing, include implementation fees, support, and any volume-based overages. Do you integrate with our ATS (e.g., Workday, Bullhorn, Jobvite, SuccessFactors)? Top platforms offer direct ATS connectivity, but depth differs. Look for bi-directional sync (read/write), stage and status updates, notes, and audit logs. Alex Coordinator supports bi-directional syncing across 33+ ATS platforms. For any vendor, validate with a sandbox test and field mapping checklist. Can we customize the interview questions, branding, and the AI's personality? Yes—on leading platforms, customization is a core requirement. You should be able to tailor interview guides by role, adjust tone and messaging, apply company branding, and configure evaluation criteria (including knockout requirements). In demos, ask to see how quickly your team can edit questions and scoring rules. How do you handle candidate cheating or fraud? Tools approach this differently. Alex Verify runs in real time, confirming identity and flagging suspicious patterns like AI-assisted answers, proxy interviewing signals, and location/VPN anomalies—while keeping a reviewable audit trail. If a vendor only does post-hoc checks, ask what gets flagged and how it's reported. What is the candidate experience like—do candidates find it off-putting? Candidate experience depends on conversational quality and flexibility. Alex reports a 92% five-star rating, driven by natural back-and-forth interviews and 24/7 availability. When evaluating any alternative, request completion-rate benchmarks, candidate feedback samples, and an opt-out path so your brand isn't put at risk.

title: Fed Decision and Big Tech Earnings: What Traders Are Watching
summary: US futures slip on AI-spending fears as traders brace for the Fed decision and Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and Amazon earnings. Alphabet's Q2 anchors the wave.
body_text: Metric Reading Hike odds this week 38% September hike odds 80% Expected outcome Wednesday No change Because the decision itself is widely expected, investors may focus more on Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's comments. Any signal about the timing of the next rate move could have a bigger impact on the market. The earnings calendar also adds to the tension. Microsoft (MSFT) , Meta Platforms, Apple, and Amazon are all scheduled to report later this week. Their results should provide a clearer picture of demand, AI investment, and capital spending across the megacap tech sector. Alphabet and Tesla reported last week, and both brought attention back to rising AI costs. That theme is likely to remain a major focus in the reports still to come. Alphabet Cloud Revenue Jumps 82% in Q2 Alphabet's latest quarter has set the benchmark for this week's earnings. According to The Motley Fool , Alphabet (GOOGL) reported Q2 revenue of $119.8 billion, up 24% from a year earlier. It was also the company's 12th straight quarter of double-digit revenue growth. Google Search and Other revenue rose 17% to $63.3 billion, while YouTube advertising revenue increased 13% to $11.1 billion. Google Cloud delivered the strongest growth. Revenue surged 82% year over year to $24.8 billion, representing roughly one-fifth of Alphabet's total revenue. Cloud operating income more than tripled to $8.8 billion, with an operating margin of 35.6%. Alphabet's total operating income increased 30%, while its overall operating margin rose two percentage points to 34%. The company has a market capitalization of around $3.9 trillion to $4.0 trillion and trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of about 24 times. At the same time, Alphabet raised its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to between $195 billion and $205 billion, mainly to fund AI infrastructure. Investors still reacted positively. According to The Motley Fool , GOOGL shares rose 2.13% on July 25, suggesting that strong growth helped offset concerns about higher spending. The Motley Fool also noted that a $10,000 investment in Alphabet ten years ago would now be worth around $84,000, equal to an annual return of roughly 24%. The market is now balancing two key factors. The Fed's rate outlook will influence the cost of funding the AI buildout, while upcoming earnings will show whether that spending is translating into stronger revenue and profit growth. With Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and Amazon still set to report, this week could determine whether concerns over AI spending become a bigger warning for tech stocks or remain a temporary source of volatility.
