title: Customer Satisfaction Metrics: Homebuilder's Essential Guide
summary: The Foundation buyer experience platform helps homebuilders sell more homes, more efficiently, to happier customers.
body_text: A lot of homebuilder leadership teams are looking at two different businesses at the same time. One business shows up in the operating report. Sales are moving. Starts are happening. Closings are landing. Revenue looks fine. The other business shows up in inboxes, review sites, text threads, and warranty callbacks. Buyers are confused about next steps. Construction updates go out inconsistently. Closing coordinators are chasing paperwork. Customer care teams are buried in status questions that never should have become tickets. That gap is where customer satisfaction metrics matter. Not as a soft brand exercise. As an operating discipline. For homebuilders, the challenge is that satisfaction rarely breaks in one place. It breaks across handoffs. Sales says one thing. Construction sends something else. Closing has a different task list. Warranty receives the frustration later. By the time leadership sees the signal, the issue has usually been expensive for both the customer and the team. Why Financial KPIs Arent Telling the Whole Story A division can hit its closing targets and still be training customers to distrust the brand. That usually starts after contract, when buyers leave the structured sales process and enter a far less coordinated experience. CRM handled the lead. Construction software tracks the job. ERP handles financial operations. But the customer relationship between those systems often runs on emails, spreadsheets, calls, personal texts, and whatever each team member remembers to send. The report looks healthy. The experience doesn't. A common pattern shows up like this: Sales is strong: contracts and closings are on pace. Operations is strained: coordinators and customer care reps spend too much time answering the same questions. Reputation starts slipping: reviews mention poor communication more than build quality. Leadership lacks context: there isn't one place to see what the customer was told, what they completed, and where friction started. None of that appears cleanly in gross margin, backlog, or cycle-time reporting. Practical rule: If a builder only measures financial output, that builder is often discovering customer experience problems after they have already turned into labor cost, review risk, and referral loss. This is why customer satisfaction metrics belong in operations, not just marketing. They show whether the buyer-to-owner journey is clear, consistent, and manageable for both sides. They also reveal whether the company is scaling through process discipline or through heroic manual follow-up. Homebuilders already measure operations. They just don't connect it to CX. Most builders are already good at tracking job progress, purchasing, variances, and close schedules. The blind spot is that customer friction gets treated as anecdotal instead of measurable. Repetitive buyer questions, confused homeowners, delayed document collection, and preventable warranty calls are all operating signals. That same mindset shows up in adjacent disciplines. Teams working to reduce inventory costs and waste don't manage inventory by gut feel. They build visibility into handoffs, timing, and exceptions. Customer experience requires the same discipline. A useful starting point is to pair classic satisfaction measures with customer engagement signals across milestones. This framework for customer engagement metrics is helpful because it pushes leaders to look beyond sentiment and into behavior. The takeaway is simple. A strong quarter doesn't automatically mean customers had a strong experience. In homebuilding, those can drift apart for a long time before the business feels the full cost. The Three Essential Survey Metrics for Homebuilders Most builders don't need more surveys. They need fewer surveys, used at the right moments. The three survey metrics that matter most are CSAT , CES , and NPS . Each answers a different question. Problems start when teams use one metric to solve every problem, or they send surveys at the wrong point in the lifecycle. CSAT works best at milestone moments Customer Satisfaction Score, or CSAT, measures how satisfied someone was with a specific interaction or milestone. For homebuilders, that makes it useful after events such as: Design center appointments: Was the process clear and organized? Loan or document collection steps: Did the buyer understand what was needed? New home orientation: Did the homeowner feel prepared? Close completion: Did the process feel coordinated? CSAT is transactional. That's its strength. It captures whether a specific part of the journey worked. What doesn't work is using CSAT months later to judge overall loyalty. By then, too many experiences have blended together, and the score stops telling leadership which team or process needs help. CES exposes friction faster than most builders expect Customer Effort Score, or CES, measures how easy or difficult it was for the customer to complete something. That is extremely valuable in homebuilding because many experience failures aren't about attitude. They're about effort. Buyers get frustrated when they have to ask twice, submit the same document again, chase an update, or call to understand what should have been obvious. CES is especially effective in areas like: Closing preparation Warranty request intake Scheduling service visits Finding home documents post-close A useful outside perspective on CES for enterprise teams reinforces the core principle: effort is often the clearest early warning that process design is failing the customer. Low effort usually means the builder has done the hard work internally. High effort usually means the customer is doing it instead. NPS should be used later, not everywhere Net Promoter Score, or NPS, is about loyalty and advocacy. In plain terms, it asks whether the buyer would recommend the builder. For a homebuilder, NPS makes the most sense after the dust settles. Not right after contract. Not while a homeowner is still waiting on punch items. It works better once the customer has lived with the experience long enough to judge the company as a whole. That makes it useful for understanding: Referral potential Long-term trust Whether the closing glow wore off quickly How post-close service is affecting brand advocacy NPS is a lagging relationship metric. It helps leadership understand if all the operational work across sales, construction, closing, and care added up to confidence. The right metric depends on the moment A simple way to use these customer satisfaction metrics is to match them to the buyer-to-owner lifecycle: Use CSAT after milestone interactions. Use CES where process friction is likely. Use NPS after the customer has enough distance to judge the relationship. Builders that get this right don't ask for feedback more often. They ask more precisely. Operational Data The True Voice of the Customer Surveys are useful. They are not enough. A buyer might ignore a survey and still call three times asking where to upload a document. A homeowner might never rate the warranty experience but still send repeated follow-ups because nobody gave a clear status update. In homebuilding, operational behavior often tells the truth sooner than survey feedback does. The cleanest signal is usually in the workflow When leaders want to understand satisfaction, they should start by asking where customers are forced to work too hard. That usually shows up in a handful of operating metrics: Time to close from contract readiness: Long delays often mean the buyer is unclear, the task flow is fragmented, or internal coordination is weak. First contact resolution in customer care: If simple issues keep bouncing, homeowners feel ignored even when the team is busy. Inbound question volume by milestone: Repeated questions usually point to missing guidance, weak updates, or inconsistent expectations. Engagement with homeowner resources: If homeowners aren't using documents, maintenance guidance, or service workflows, the experience may be hard to access or poorly introduced. These aren't just efficiency measures. They are customer satisfaction metrics in operational form. When a builder says, "customers keep asking the same thing," that's not noise. That's a design flaw in communication. Operational metrics are harder to game Survey scores can be distorted by timing, low response volume, or the personality of one team member. Operational data is less forgiving. If a closing team is constantly chasing tasks or a warranty team spends its day giving status updates instead of resolving issues, the underlying process is telling leadership exactly where the friction sits. Customer data discipline proves vital. Teams evaluating customer record quality can learn something from tools built for adjacent real estate workflows, such as a RealEstateCRM platform for agents . The lesson isn't the product category. It's the importance of having consistent data, visible touchpoints, and a usable customer record across the journey. For builders, warranty is often the sharpest example. A low survey response rate can hide serious homeowner frustration, but a backlog of preventable callbacks can't. A better lens on that issue starts with the broader warranty experience , especially how intake, routing, updates, and accountability shape trust after closing. The best programs use both forms of listening Surveys answer, "How did the customer say they felt?" Operational data answers, "What did the customer have to do?" Builders need both. But if leadership has to choose where to start, operational friction is often the faster path to action. It shows where teams are spending time, where buyers are losing confidence, and where homeowners begin to question whether anyone owns the relationship. Framework for Measuring Homebuilder Satisfaction Most builders don't have a measurement problem. They have a consistency problem. Different teams track different things, in different systems, with different definitions. Sales may own milestone surveys. Closing may track readiness in spreadsheets. Construction may log updates in another platform. Customer care may manage service activity somewhere else. Leadership then gets partial answers and no shared operating view. A practical measurement model starts with one rule. Every metric must connect to an owner, a workflow, and a business decision. What a usable framework looks like A solid framework includes both survey metrics and operational proxies. It also avoids fake precision. "Top quartile" performance isn't one universal number for every builder, market, or product type. A realistic benchmark is qualitative and directional: Leading: the metric is consistently reviewed, trusted, and used to trigger action. Maturing: the metric exists, but ownership or data quality is uneven. Lagging: the metric is anecdotal, delayed, or trapped in one department. The reference table below is a practical audit tool. Metric What It Measures Data Source Benchmark (Top Quartile) CSAT by milestone Satisfaction with a specific interaction such as design, orientation, or close Survey tool, CRM, closing workflow platform Consistently captured at key milestones with comments reviewed and routed quickly CES for closing tasks How easy it is for buyers to complete pre-close actions Closing workflow platform, survey tool, communication logs Buyers report the process is easy, and teams see fewer repetitive questions CES for warranty intake How easy it is for homeowners to submit and track service issues Customer care platform, intake forms, service request workflow Homeowners can submit issues clearly, receive updates, and avoid status-chasing NPS post-close Willingness to recommend the builder after living in the home Survey tool, homeowner database, post-close outreach workflows Used as a true relationship measure, with clear follow-up on detractors and promoter activation Inbound question volume Whether communication is proactive enough to prevent repetitive outreach Shared inboxes, call logs, SMS, communication platform Question volume is stable and concentrated on true exceptions, not basic process confusion Time to close readiness Whether buyers move through post-contract and closing steps without avoidable delay CRM, ERP, closing checklist tools, title and lender coordination workflows Tasks move predictably, and exceptions are visible early rather than surfacing late First contact resolution in warranty Whether customer care resolves issues without repeated homeowner effort Customer care platform, case notes, vendor coordination workflows Common issues are resolved cleanly, with minimal back-and-forth and strong accountability Homeowner resource engagement Whether owners use documents, maintenance guidance, and support resources Homeowner portal, document hub, post-close communication platform Homeowners actively use self-service resources, reducing avoidable inbound traffic Review and referral signals Whether experience quality is translating into reputation and advocacy Review monitoring, referral workflows, homeowner marketing systems Positive advocacy is visible and linked to lifecycle experience, not left to chance Ownership matters more than formula purity Plenty of teams get stuck debating calculation methods. That matters less than ownership and response. For example: Sales or closing leaders should own transactional milestone feedback that reflects handoff quality. Construction leaders should care about question volume tied to update consistency. Customer care leaders should own effort, resolution, and homeowner communication after close. Division leadership should review the full picture, not isolated departmental numbers. A related resource on how to measure customer engagement is useful here because engagement often exposes whether customers are using the information and tools the builder provides. Leadership test: If a score drops, can someone name the process owner, the likely cause, and the first corrective action? If not, the metric isn't operational yet. The point of a framework isn't to build a prettier report. It's to make customer satisfaction metrics usable across the buyer-to-owner lifecycle. Designing Your Homebuilder CX Dashboard A useful dashboard should help a COO or division president answer three questions quickly. Where is friction building. Which teams or communities need attention. What should be fixed first. Most dashboards fail because they show isolated metrics instead of connected cause and effect. Leadership sees survey scores in one report, warranty workload in another, and closing delays somewhere else. That makes it hard to spot the pattern behind the number. Build the dashboard around the lifecycle The best homebuilder CX dashboards follow the customer journey, not the org chart. A practical dashboard view should include: Post-contract health: task completion, milestone communication, buyer question volume, and transactional satisfaction. Pre-close readiness: document completion, unresolved exceptions, orientation feedback, and close risk indicators. Post-close service health: intake effort, open request visibility, resolution flow, and homeowner follow-up load. Longer-term relationship health: recommendation intent, review patterns, referral activity, and homeowner engagement. This structure matters because it lets leadership see how one breakdown creates another. Weak communication before close often becomes lower trust after close. Poor homeowner education often turns into unnecessary warranty traffic. Use leading and lagging indicators together A strong dashboard mixes leading indicators and lagging indicators . Leading indicators tell leaders where a problem is forming. Lagging indicators confirm what the experience felt like once the customer judged it. Here is a simple way to consider it: Dashboard Layer Example Indicators Leadership Use Leading Buyer question spikes, low task completion, hard warranty intake, slow first response Catch friction before it damages trust broadly Lagging NPS themes, review sentiment, repeat complaints, referral softness Confirm whether operational fixes are changing the relationship A dashboard also needs drill-down capability. Portfolio-level health is useful, but leaders also need views by division, community, stage, and team. Without that, the dashboard stays interesting but not actionable. A more complete view of what a connected lifecycle system can support is outlined in this look at a homebuilder customer engagement platform . The key idea is straightforward. Builders don't need another isolated report. They need visibility across the customer relationship after the sale begins. A good dashboard doesn't just show that customers are unhappy. It shows where the operating model made that outcome likely. Actionable Playbooks to Improve Your Scores Scores only matter if they change behavior. When a builder sees weak customer satisfaction metrics, the fix usually isn't "send more surveys" or "coach the team to be nicer." The fix is to remove friction from the operating model. That means improving handoffs, reducing repetitive work, clarifying ownership, and giving customers one clear path instead of five inconsistent ones. If post-contract CSAT is slipping Buyers usually aren't reacting to one bad email. They're reacting to uncertainty. What to do next Standardize milestone communication. Every buyer should receive the same core updates at the same moments, regardless of community or coordinator. Create one place for tasks and documents. Stop making buyers search inboxes for what they need to complete. Audit the sales-to-closing handoff. Confirm promises, dates, contacts, and next-step instructions are consistent. Track question themes weekly. Repeated confusion points should trigger process edits, not just better call handling. In this operational context, post-contract experience tools like Closing Concierge are well-suited. They help builders centralize tasks, visibility, and buyer communication before close. If warranty CES is weak A low effort score in warranty usually means homeowners are doing too much work just to be heard. Operational response Tighten intake: use structured request capture so teams receive complete issue details from the start. Automate acknowledgments and status updates: homeowners shouldn't need to ask if anyone saw their request. Separate simple from complex cases: triage prevents routine issues from clogging the same queue as serious escalations. Make vendor coordination visible: internal teams need to know what is pending, assigned, scheduled, or blocked. An AI-accelerated customer care platform like WarrantyOS is relevant here because automation should remove repetitive work so teams can spend more time on judgment, empathy, and resolution. Homeowners don't judge warranty on internal effort. They judge it on clarity, responsiveness, and whether the issue moved without constant chasing. If NPS is flat even when milestone scores look fine That usually means the builder is delivering decent transactions but not a consistent relationship. Try this playbook: Review the whole journey, not just touchpoints. The customer remembers the gaps between teams as much as the individual interactions. Map detractor comments to operating stages. Look for themes tied to move-in, early ownership, or unresolved service friction. Strengthen post-close education. Home documents, maintenance guidance, and product information should be easy to find and easy to use. Create referral moments intentionally. Satisfied owners rarely become advocates by accident. If teams need practical ideas for loyalty improvement, this guide on how to improve NPS scores is a strong next read because it ties advocacy to process design, not just outreach. If inbound question volume stays high This is often the simplest signal in the business. Customers are telling the builder what communication failed. Focus on three moves: Rewrite the top unclear messages. Trigger updates before customers ask. Give every team access to the same customer timeline. That reduces manual follow-up, protects team capacity, and creates a more consistent builder-branded experience from contract through ownership. Foundation is built for homebuilders that want to connect the buyer-to-owner lifecycle without replacing the systems already running sales, construction, financials, or service. It gives teams a dedicated customer experience layer to standardize communication, automate repetitive work, improve lifecycle visibility, and support a builder-branded journey from contract through closing, warranty, ownership, referrals, and repeat purchase. For leaders focused on reducing manual communication and modernizing customer care, Foundation is worth a closer look.

summary: WISeKey Reports Unaudited Preliminary H1 2026 Key Metrics; Revenue Up 115%, FY 2026 Guidance Reaffirmed FY 2026 guidance of 50%–100% revenue growth underpinned by an active pipeline exceeding $225 million through 2029, new business initiatives and approximately $495 million in cash and short-term investments. body_text: WISeKey Reports Unaudited Preliminary H1 2026 Key Metrics; Revenue Up 115%, FY 2026 Guidance Reaffirmed FY 2026 guidance of 50%–100% revenue growth underpinned by an active pipeline exceeding $225 million through 2029, new business initiatives and approximately $495 million in cash and short-term investments. Demonstrates continued execution across its quantum, space and digital identity platforms, highlighted by the filing of Form F-4 for the WISeSat–Columbus Acquisition Corp business combination, the launch of operations of Quantix, a post-quantum identity partnership with Wecan, and the integration of the WISeKey Quantum RootKey across SEALQuantum assets. Geneva, Switzerland – July 13, 2026 – Ad hoc announcement pursuant to Art. 53 LR WISeKey International Holding Ltd (“WISeKey” or the “Company”) (SIX: WIHN; Nasdaq: WKEY), a global leader in cybersecurity, digital identity, post-quantum semiconductors and satellite technology, today announced preliminary unaudited financial highlights for the six months ended June 30, 2026, (“H1”) together with a summary of the key strategic milestones achieved year to date. Preliminary figures are unaudited and subject to completion of the Company’s half-year closing procedures. WISeKey expects to publish its full H1 2026 consolidated financial results in September 2026 and hold a half-year earnings conference call. Preliminary H1 2026 Financial Highlights (Unaudited) Preliminary H1 2026 revenue of approximately $11.4 million , an increase of 115% versus H1 2025 revenue, underscoring strong operating momentum across the group’s post-quantum semiconductor, digital identity and PKI businesses. Approximately $495 million in cash and short-term investments as of June 30, 2026, representative of a very strong balance sheet with zero debt, allowing for WISeKey’s subsidiary SEALSQ to fund their post-quantum, quantum and Quantum Space Orbital Cloud (QSOC) roadmaps without near-term financing pressure. Subsidiary SEALSQ has an active commercial pipeline exceeding $225 million through 2029 , driven by demand for post-quantum cryptography solutions ahead of regulatory migration deadlines in the U.S. and Europe. These figures reflect management estimates and are subject to risks such as conversion risks, customer validation, and technical integration. FY 2026 guidance reaffirmed: supported by its cash position and pipeline visibility, the Company reiterates its expectations of 50%–100% revenue growth in FY 2026 . Our guidance statements are based on current expectations. These statements are forward-looking and actual results could differ materially depending on market conditions and the factors set forth under “Forward Looking Statements” below. The balance sheet reflects SEALSQ’s successful capital markets activity, including a $125 million registered direct offering completed in March 2026, and disciplined treasury management at the holding level. Key Strategic Milestones — First Half of 2026 Quantisimo potential business combination. In June 2026, WISeKey and SEALSQ established Quantisimo Corp. as a special purpose vehicle and executed a non-binding Letter of Intent with GigCapital8 Corp. to create a publicly traded quantum computing company at an initial enterprise value of $575 million, with the aim of consolidating selected assets from the group’s SEALQuantum.com initiative into a single Nasdaq-listed entity. The transaction is targeted to close in the first quarter of 2027. WISeSat: Form F-4 filed for Nasdaq listing via business combination with Columbus Acquisition Corp. On June 23, 2026, WISeSat.Space Holdings Corp. (“Pubco”), a wholly owned subsidiary of WISeSat.Space Corp. (“WISeSat”), filed a registration statement on Form F-4 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission in connection with the previously announced business combination with Columbus Acquisition Corp (“CAC”; Nasdaq: COLA), governed by the Business Combination Agreement dated November 9, 2025 among WISeSat, CAC, Pubco, WISeKey and WISeSat Merger Sub Corp. Upon completion of the transaction, which remains subject to the registration statement being declared effective by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”), the approval of CAC shareholders, and Nasdaq approval of the listing of Pubco’s registered shares, WISeSat and CAC will each become subsidiaries of Pubco, with the combined company expected to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “SAIQ”. The WISeSat constellation continued its deployment cadence during the period with additional satellite launches via SpaceX. Quantix: start of operations. Quantix Edge Security (“Quantix”), the group’s Spanish joint venture dedicated to the development of a Semiconductor Design and Personnalization Center in the region of Murcia, Spain, with advanced capabilities in cybersecurity, post-quantum technology, AI and RISC-V systems, confirmed the selection of the Region of Murcia as the location for the center. Quantix commenced operations during the first half of 2026 and will now begin an in-depth technical verification phase together with the relevant public administrations aimed at defining the operational, administrative and infrastructure related aspects necessary for the project’s development. Post-quantum identity technology in partnership with Wecan. WISeKey entered a technology partnership with Wecan Group (“Wecan”), the Geneva-based leader in regulated data exchange and tokenization infrastructure and a subsidiary of SEALSQ, to develop post-quantum cryptography (PQC) enabled digital identity technology. The collaboration combines WISeKey’s WISeID platform, PKI trust services and SEALSQ’s post-quantum secure semiconductors with Wecan’s compliance and data-sovereignty infrastructure, targeting quantum-resistant identity solutions for financial institutions and regulated industries. Integration of the WISeKey Quantum RootKey across SEALQuantum assets. WISeKey commenced the integration of its Quantum RootKey, the post-quantum evolution of the cryptographic Root of Trust operated under the OISTE Foundation governance model since 1999, across the SEALQuantum.com ecosystem of quantum technology companies. The integration anchors each SEALQuantum asset to a common, quantum-resistant trust infrastructure, extending the group’s Root-to-Qubit architecture from semiconductors to the full quantum ecosystem. Regulatory tailwinds for SEALSQ’s post-quantum semiconductors. SEALSQ’s QS7001 post-quantum secure element is aligned with the new ANSSI post-quantum cryptography mandate, positioning the company as an early mover in EU regulation-driven hardware security, while U.S. Executive Order 14412 directed the migration of federal high-value systems to post-quantum cryptography by 2030, a structural demand driver for the group’s PQC portfolio. Quantum ecosystem expansion. During the period, SEALSQ completed the acquisition of MiraEx, the Swiss developer of photonics-based quantum interconnects, and co-led the $130 million Series A financing of Quobly alongside Bpifrance and STMicroelectronics, further strengthening the Company’s quantum portfolio. SEALCOIN: market launch and QAIT token integration. In May 2026, WISeKey’s SEALCOIN platform confirmed the integration of the QAIT token following its market launch, advancing the group’s machine-economy strategy for autonomous device-to-device transactions secured by the post-quantum Root of Trust. WISeRobot: human-centric AI robotics roadmap. In May 2026, WISeKey and SEALSQ announced the roadmap and official website launch of WISeRobot.ch, integrating human-centric AI with post-quantum security in robotics and extending the group’s trust architecture into autonomous systems. WISeSat investment in FOSSA Systems. In June 2026, WISeSat.Space participated in FOSSA Systems’ latest financing round, reinforcing its European secure satellite infrastructure roadmap. HUMAN-AI-T initiative. WISeKey’s founder launched the HUMAN-AI-T Manifesto through the OISTE Foundation at Davos in January 2026 and, in May 2026, expanded the initiative into a global movement calling for ethical, human-governed AI, including the development of the HUMAN-AI-T Knowledge Vault — advancing the group’s commitment to trust, identity and the defense of the human person in the age of AI. Corporate & Governance Updates Corporate redomiciliation to the British Virgin Islands. On June 29, 2026, WISeKey signed a merger agreement to redomicile the holding company from Switzerland to the British Virgin Islands. Additional information regarding the proposed transaction will be contained in the registration statement on Form F-4 that WISeKey intends to file with the SEC. 2026 Annual General Meeting. At the Annual General Meeting held on June 29, 2026, shareholders approved all agenda items proposed by the Board of Directors, including the Annual Report 2025, the re-election of seven current directors and the election of Andrew Forson as a new member of the Board. Management Commentary “With first-half revenue up 115% versus H1 2025 revenue and approximately $495 million in cash and short-term investments, WISeKey enters the second half of 2026 from a position of strength, growing fast, fully funded, and with a pipeline exceeding USD 225 million through 2029 in SEALSQ,” said Carlos Creus Moreira, Founder and CEO of WISeKey. “In the last six months we have signed the non-binding LOI for the Quantisimo transaction with GigCapital8, filed the Form F-4 for the WISeSat listing, brought Quantix into operation, partnered with Wecan on post-quantum identity, and begun anchoring every SEALQuantum asset to our Quantum RootKey. Together these milestones advance a single strategy: extending the Root of Trust we built in Geneva over 25 years into the quantum era, from the chip, to the satellite, to the identity of every human and machine, positioning WISeKey to capture long-term value for shareholders.” About WISeKey WISeKey International Holding Ltd (“WISeKey”, SIX: WIHN; Nasdaq: WKEY) is a global leader in cybersecurity, digital identity, and Internet of Things (IoT) solutions. Operating as a Swiss-based holding company through several operational subsidiaries — including SEALSQ Corp (Nasdaq: LAES) for post-quantum semiconductors, WISeSat for LEO satellite connectivity, WISeKey SA for the WISeID digital identity ecosystem, and SEALCOIN for machine-economy transactional technology — each subsidiary contributes to WISeKey’s integrated cryptographic Root of Trust, operated under the neutral governance of the OISTE Foundation. For more information, visit www.wisekey.com. title: Avo speaks Figma now
summary: Introducing the Avo Figma integration for Journeys
body_text: Picture this: your designer (agent) just dropped a new flow in Figma. You want to plan tracking for it on Avo, but the screens are stuck in Figma. So you start the chore. Multi-select the frames you want, export PNGs, save locally, switch to Avo, find the files again, drag and drop them in, reorder them based on where they sat in the design file, then connect the journey steps. You haven't started the actual tracking work yet. Today we're shipping the Avo Figma integration. Paste a Figma link into a journey, and the screens land where they belong. You get to start with the part that matters. And we're not done. AI-assisted journey design has already started landing in Avo, and there's more coming. Our MCP will bring the same workflow to the AI tools your team already uses. More on both soon. Why we built Journeys, and why this changes things For teams not using Avo Journeys, the first pass of data design still happens outside the tracking plan, in screenshots, FigJam boards, and scratch docs. PMs sketch the user flows but rarely write the specs themselves. Analysts translate those flows into events and properties by hand, becoming a bottleneck the whole team waits on. Engineers implement against descriptions, not the screens themselves. Three people, three versions of the picture, resulting in dashboards nobody fully trusts. The fix is obvious in hindsight: design tracking on top of the actual screens. Use the design as the structure for the flow, attach tracking decisions to the moments that matter, and keep everyone looking at the same picture. That was the idea behind Journeys , which we launched last December. As one PM put it after using it: "What's great about Journeys is you're really talking about the visual definition of what's going on. You stop describing flows in Slack and start pointing at them." Journeys gave teams a way to plan, review, and implement tracking with the user flow visible the whole time. PMs could contribute. Engineers got specs tied to specific screens. Reviewers had context. Tracking design stopped feeling like a translation exercise. But every one of those benefits came with a tax that teams paid up front, before the workflow could start paying back. Today's release takes that tax to zero, and Journeys stops being a workflow teams have to deliberately invest in. The friction we couldn't ignore Every journey started with somebody manually exporting screens from Figma, frame by frame, and rearranging them in Avo to match the original layout. We heard the same thing in conversation after conversation. Getting designs into Avo was too manual, with too many clicks. As one Product Manager put it: "It takes a lot of time to basically add the design and then recreate the flow inside Avo." Even when teams pushed through the import, the journey didn't stay current. A designer would update a frame, the journey wouldn't, and the screens in Avo turned into a snapshot from whenever someone last took the time to re-export. The Figma integration has been the most-requested improvement to Journeys since we shipped it. How it actually feels to use Here's the new flow. You're in Avo, starting a journey for a new feature. Instead of opening Figma in another tab to begin the export ritual, you switch to Figma, copy a link to a frame, section or page, and switch back to Avo. Paste anywhere on the canvas. The screens land in your journey, with their frame names as step titles, in their real layout, ready for the actual tracking work. A single frame link drops in as a step where you pasted it. Section and file links open a frame picker that mirrors your Figma canvas, with thumbnails arranged in the same spatial positions you laid them out in. Pick the frames that matter for this journey, hit Import, and they arrive with the layout preserved. Frames that sat in the same row in Figma come in already connected, so the horizontal flow you drew in your design file shows up as a connected journey from the start. The part we find most quietly satisfying is what happens after the import. Every step keeps a link back to its original frame. Hover any step to jump straight to Figma, or hit Reload from Figma to pull the latest version when the design has moved on. Journeys stop being snapshots. They stay in step with the design file they came from. What this unlocks The Figma integration removes a chore. The bigger shift is what becomes possible when journeys are cheap to build and easy to keep current. Designers and PMs start using Avo because the entry point is a Figma link they already had open, not a tracking plan they had to learn first. Reviewers see the screens designers are actually shipping. Engineers get code snippets tied to specific screens, with the design context still attached, so there's no ambiguity about which event fires where. The Plan, Review, Implement loop your team already runs keeps its shape. The piece that used to fall off the table (keeping the visual context in sync with reality) is taken care of. How to get started The Figma integration is available to all Avo customers at no additional cost. Connect Figma from Settings → Integrations → Figma and any teammate can start pasting links into journeys. The connection is a one-time setup. Read the docs for a walkthrough . If you're new to Avo, this is a good moment to take a look. Journeys plus the Figma integration is the cleanest workflow we've built for designing analytics from the ground up, and you can sign up for free to try it on your own files. If you're already using Avo and want help rolling it out, reach out at support@avo.app. This is the first step in connecting your design tools to your tracking plan. There's more we want to do here. Tell us what we should build next.

title: Celebrating 25 years of visual search innovation
summary: Google Images is turning 25. Here’s a look back at some major milestones — and new ways to explore and create visual content.
body_text: Celebrating 25 years of visual search innovation Jul 14, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail We're celebrating Google Images turning 25 with a look back at some major milestones — and introducing new ways to explore and create visual content. Brad Kellett Senior Engineering Director, Search Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental This week marks 25 years since we launched Google Images , beginning the evolution of Search from a text-based experience to one that allows you to visually explore the world. To celebrate this milestone, we’re introducing two new ways to help you explore and create visual content — plus a look back at our major innovations in visual search. Explore images in a whole new way. Today, we're introducing a brand new browseable home for Google Images , featuring a dynamic, immersive gallery of images from across the web — updated in real time and intelligently tailored to your unique interests. As you browse and save ideas to your collections , they’ll appear as tabs above the main gallery, making it easy to jump back in and continue exploring based on what inspires you. This will roll out over the coming weeks on desktop in the U.S. in English. Sign in to your Google Account to try it out. Create new images right in Search. Sometimes, the perfect image is out there on the web, waiting to be found. But other times you might have a highly specific vision where an image doesn’t yet exist. To help bring those unique ideas to life, we’re bringing image generation directly into AI Overviews in Search. Using our latest Nano Banana model , this update transforms a simple text prompt into a high-quality, custom visual made completely from scratch, seamlessly bridging the gap between imagination and reality. Image generation in AI Overviews will start to roll out over the coming weeks in English, for all regions that currently support image creation in AI Mode . Both of these updates are built on 25 years of innovation to make the world’s visual information instantly accessible and useful. To see how we got here, let’s take a look back at some of the major launches that transformed how we search with — and for — images. 2001: Google Images When Jennifer Lopez’s iconic green Versace dress broke the internet in 2000, we realized that the standard search page at the time — a list of blue text links — simply wasn’t enough. People didn’t just want to read about the dress — they wanted to see it. So in July 2001, we launched Google Images, making it possible for the first time to search and instantly explore visual content from across the web. 2009: Similar Images The Similar Images feature made it possible to find pictures without relying on text alone. If you searched for “bow,” you might see images of hair bows and bows and arrows. By clicking the one you had in mind and tapping “find similar images,” you could see more of what you wanted without typing a whole new query. 2011: Search by Image We launched Search by Image to change how you navigate the web — moving beyond text to let the image do the work for you. By simply uploading an image or pasting its URL directly into the search bar, visuals became search terms. This allowed you to quickly identify the original source, track down where the photo appeared across the web or discover visually similar content. 2018: Google Lens in Search Google Lens makes your everyday life searchable, letting you use your smartphone camera to ask about the world around you. With Lens, you can identify objects, translate text and pull up product links in real time without typing a query into the search box. 2022: Multisearch in Lens Multisearch marked a significant step into the era of multimodal search. Now, you can search with text and images at the same time, like snapping a photo of a unique landmark and adding “what inspired this design.” Or taking a picture of a sleek dining table you saw on social and typing “coffee table” to find a similar piece for your own home. 2024: Circle to Search To help you search anything on your Android phone screen, we built Circle to Search . With a simple gesture — like circling, highlighting, scribbling or tapping — you can select what you’re curious about on your phone screen and get more information right in the moment, without switching apps. Circle to Search is available on more than 580 million Android devices around the world. 2025: Lens + AI Mode Last year, we brought together the multimodal power of Lens with AI Mode in Search so you can ask even more nuanced questions that require deeper reasoning. When you upload or snap a photo, AI Mode can process the entire scene. Using a " visual image fan-out " technique, it breaks a single image search into dozens of sub-queries to understand the full visual context and deliver relevant results. 2025: Search Live Building on our advanced multimodal capabilities, Search Live lets you share your phone’s live camera feed while having an interactive voice conversation in AI Mode — using video input to capture motion and the full context of your surroundings. It’s like having a video call with Search — great for everything from help in the kitchen to troubleshooting tricky equipment. 2025: Visual Results in AI Mode To make visual exploration feel more natural, we introduced an entirely new way to explore, imagine and shop using AI Mode in Search. You can describe exactly what you have in mind in a conversational way — like asking for "barrel jeans that aren't too baggy" — to instantly pull up a grid of visual inspiration and shoppable products. 2026: Circle to Search Multi-Object Recognition Circle to Search now lets you explore multiple objects within a single image all at once, using the visual image fan-out technique. You can instantly deconstruct and shop for an entire outfit or search multiple items in one scene simultaneously to learn about what you see. 2026: Intelligent Search Box With the new intelligent search box , you can now ask detailed questions about images right in Search and get a helpful AI Mode response. Just tap the plus icon to upload images — even multiple at a time — and ask whatever’s on your mind. Over the last 25 years, Search has grown from helping you find a specific photo on the web to helping you search the world, exactly as you see — or imagine — it. We’ve come a long way and we’re excited to continue pushing the boundaries of what’s possible in visual search. Build a Website Accessibility Strategy That Welcomes More People
summary: Create a practical website accessibility strategy that improves readability, supports keyboard navigation, strengthens inclusivity, and makes accessibility reviews repeatable.
body_text: Build a Website Accessibility Strategy That Welcomes More People An accessible site does not begin with a compliance checklist or end with a single scan. It begins when a business asks whether every person can understand the message, move through the page, and complete the intended task without an unnecessary barrier. A website accessibility strategy turns that question into a steady, practical habit. This work benefits people using screen readers, keyboards, voice controls, zoomed text, a small phone, a slow connection, or simply a noisy and distracting environment. Improving readability for every visitor and supporting keyboard-friendly navigation often make a site clearer for everyone. The result is not a special version of the website; it is a better default experience. Start by mapping barriers, not labels Strikingly Website Builder A useful website accessibility strategy looks at a real visitor goal. Can someone find the service, understand the offer, select a product option, send a question, or read an article without having to work around the design? Begin with the pages where a visitor must make a decision, not only the homepage. A five-minute barrier map Open the page at a larger text size and check whether improving readability for every visitor still leaves a calm, usable layout. Use only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, and Space to see whether supporting keyboard-friendly navigation reaches every meaningful control. Read headings and buttons without relying on nearby imagery; this is part of enhancing website inclusivity standards for people using assistive tools. Check whether the page explains errors, pricing, delivery, or next steps in words, not color alone. Record one obstacle and one owner before moving to the next page; meeting accessibility best practices needs accountable follow-through. The Strikingly accessibility guide is a practical starting point for alt text, headings, readable fonts, contrast, and captions. It also makes an important distinction: platform tools can help, but a website owner remains responsible for the content and local requirements that apply to the site. A website accessibility strategy is therefore an operating practice, not a legal promise. Make the map with a colleague who did not build the page, or invite feedback from people who use different devices and assistive technologies. Enhancing website inclusivity standards is stronger when it is informed by actual experience rather than assumptions about what visitors find easy. A mature website accessibility strategy gives each important barrier an owner and a deadline. Enhancing website inclusivity standards requires design, content, and customer-facing teams to share what they learn. Meeting accessibility best practices becomes more realistic when a small fix can be completed before the next campaign instead of waiting for a full rebuild. Make meaning easy to see and hear App Dream Template from Strikingly Improving readability for every visitor means more than increasing font size. Visitors need short paragraphs, honest headings, predictable labels, adequate contrast, and enough space to separate ideas. A dense page may be technically readable yet still exhausting when someone is scanning on a phone or processing information slowly. Use headings to describe the next question a visitor has, rather than styling a sentence to look like a heading. This gives screen-reader users a useful outline and helps everyone skim. Improving readability for every visitor also means writing buttons that say what happens next: "View plans," "Send my question," or "Read the guide" are clearer than a vague "Learn more." Images need an equally deliberate decision. If an image communicates information, add concise alt text that describes its purpose in context. If it is purely decorative, do not make it a detour. Strikingly's image tools and the section editor make it easier to keep words, visuals, and page structure aligned. Meeting accessibility best practices means checking the published page, not merely assuming the editor settings are enough. Use the keyboard path as a customer journey Strikingly Alt Text Editor Supporting keyboard-friendly navigation is one of the clearest ways to find interaction problems. Start at the browser address bar, press Tab, and observe the order in which focus moves. Can you always see where you are? Can you open navigation, use filters, close an overlay, submit a form, and return to the content without a mouse? Supporting keyboard-friendly navigation is not just about reaching a button eventually. The order should follow the page's visual and logical order. A hidden focus state, a modal that traps the visitor, or a menu that skips a key option turns a straightforward task into friction. Test the same path on a mobile-sized browser window because responsive changes can alter control order. For conversion pages, move through the inquiry flow with the keyboard before publishing. Review each field in a custom form , the confirmation message, and the next useful action. Supporting keyboard-friendly navigation should allow a person to recover from an error and understand what must be corrected, not just reach the submit control. Clear page structure helps this path. Use Site Search for content-heavy sites, keep menu labels descriptive, and give buttons a visible purpose. Enhancing website inclusivity standards is often the same as reducing uncertainty for a busy visitor who has no disability at all. Supporting keyboard-friendly navigation should be retested whenever a new menu, embedded tool, pop-up, or campaign form is added. No website accessibility strategy should call a page finished until its main action can be started, changed, and completed without a pointer. Meeting accessibility best practices includes preserving a visible focus state while still keeping the page visually calm. Prioritize changes by visitor risk Strikingly Contact Form Not every issue needs the same response. A missing description on a decorative image is different from a checkout form that cannot be completed with a keyboard. A good website accessibility strategy groups work by the degree to which it prevents a core task, then fixes the most harmful barriers first. Fix first: barriers to information and action Improving readability for every visitor comes first when text blends into its background, is too small to read, or relies on color to show status. Supporting keyboard-friendly navigation comes first when a visitor cannot use a menu, form, checkout step, pop-up, or close control. Enhancing website inclusivity standards comes first when essential information appears only in an image, video, or ambiguous icon. Meeting accessibility best practices comes first when a page change creates a new barrier for a key audience or service. Next, resolve issues that create confusion or extra effort: repeated instructions, unclear error messages, jargon-heavy copy, or a comparison that only works when someone can interpret a color scale. Improving readability for every visitor can be tested with a short content review. Ask whether a first-time visitor can say what the page offers, who it is for, and what happens after they choose an action. When updating a page, preview it on desktop and mobile before it goes live. Strikingly's button settings , pop-up controls , and blog tools can support a clear visitor flow. Meeting accessibility best practices requires the same care for a campaign landing page, a product page, and a supporting article. Make accessibility part of ordinary publishing The most durable website accessibility strategy is small enough to use every time. Add a short accessibility review to the same publishing routine that checks links, spelling, mobile appearance, and analytics. This avoids the costly pattern of discovering dozens of barriers only during a redesign. Before each major update, use this release check: Read the page at 200 percent zoom to confirm improving readability for every visitor has not broken the hierarchy or hidden a call to action. Use the keyboard through the intended task to confirm supporting keyboard-friendly navigation from entry to completion. Review headings, alt text, captions, labels, and error messages to keep enhancing website inclusivity standards specific and useful. Check contrast and responsive behavior, then record the result so meeting accessibility best practices becomes a visible team expectation. Use analytics to notice pages that receive traffic but have unusually low engagement, then review whether the journey is understandable. Built-in Analytics and Google Analytics 4 can identify candidates for review, but visitor feedback explains the barrier. Improving readability for every visitor and supporting keyboard-friendly navigation should be checked with people, not only reports. Use the same review after changing a headline, image, or form. Improving readability for every visitor protects the meaning of new content as it is published. A website accessibility strategy should make accessibility questions routine: Can the page be understood without color? Can a keyboard user reach the decision point? Are new visuals described? Enhancing website inclusivity standards means treating those questions as part of quality, while meeting accessibility best practices means recording and resolving the answers. Keep the strategy human A website accessibility strategy works when it respects a visitor's time and independence. Enhancing website inclusivity standards means avoiding the assumption that one device, one sense, or one browsing style is normal. Supporting keyboard-friendly navigation creates a more reliable route through interactions. Improving readability for every visitor gives people a fair chance to understand before they decide. Enhancing website inclusivity standards also means preserving supporting keyboard-friendly navigation as new content and features are added. Meeting accessibility best practices is an ongoing commitment, not a finish line. A website accessibility strategy should review the pages that matter most, fix barriers to real tasks, and include accessibility in every new piece of content. Enhancing website inclusivity standards keeps this work centered on people, while meeting accessibility best practices leaves the site easier to improve tomorrow.

title: Opera is the first browser to natively protect you from clipboard attacks – Introducing Paste Protect
summary: We’re introducing "Paste Protect:" a feature that protects you from code injection attacks such as ClickFix.
body_text: Hey all, Today we’re introducing a unique browser-native feature that protects you from malicious code injection attacks such as ClickFix: we’re calling it ‘Paste Protect. What are malicious code injections? you may ask. Basically, they are attacks that use social engineering to trick you into allowing attackers access to your system or sensitive data. What we’re introducing today into Opera One, on Early Bird mode, is a feature that prevents these attacks in two ways: It actively prevents the malicious code from being copied onto your clipboard. It lets you know that there was an attempt to copy something onto your clipboard that’s potentially harmful. This means that if you’re accessing a website that is trying to copy something potentially harmful into your clipboard (or luring you into doing so), Opera will detect it, prevent it, and let you know about it. We’re the first major browser to integrate a feature that protects you from this type of attacks natively. While there are extensions that try to do the same, and warning systems are featured in some operating systems, Paste Protect is built directly into the Opera browser – the first line of defense before a malicious command even makes it that far into your machine. We take your security very seriously so we’re constantly keeping up with the latest trends and threats to help you work on your projects and begin new ones with peace of mind. If you want to know more about how these attacks work, what a ClickFix-based attack is, and how Opera is protecting you from them, we’ve prepared an article for you and you can access it here . What kind of attacks does Opera protect you from With this update Opera now protects you from ClickFix attacks which you can encounter while browsing the web. For example, when you try to get to a website and encounter the familiar “verify you’re a human” popup, or the CAPTCHA that requires you to identify traffic signs or something similar. After you tick the box confirming you’re human, or complete the CAPTCHA, a second verification prompt like the following one could pop up in your screen: When this prompt appears, the website has already “copied” something to your clipboard, and now it instructs you to open the Windows Run dialog box (Win+R), then use “Ctrl + V” to paste the malicious code, and then click “OK.” This would execute the code and compromise your device, and the data on it. Opera’s new Paste Protect feature prevents this kind of attack by directly blocking the malicious code from being copied on your clipboard in the first place, and also warns you about the situation. The best thing to do if you encounter this situation is to directly close the tab where the second popup appeared. Just to be clear, and to put us all on the same page: the clipboard is a temporary storage area on your device that holds content you’ve copied until you’re ready to paste it somewhere else. Every time you manually copy and paste or use keyboard shortcuts such as Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V (or Cmd+C and Cmd+V on Mac), you’re using the clipboard. How Opera is protecting you against malicious code injection When there is something copied to your clipboard, the Opera browser checks the content for potential threats and harmful commands. If a potential threat is detected, Opera will automatically block the capability for the browser to copy something onto your clipboard from the malicious website and provide you with the option to close the site safely. Additionally, a red warning icon will appear in the address bar as well as a popup indicating that a threat was blocked, and we’ll recommend that you close the website. This approach prevents the issue, and helps you grow awareness about it. If you’re curious about what was copied on your clipboard, you can see it in the popup that appears by clicking on ‘Show Content’ and if you’re sure about what it is and want to copy it, you can use the ‘Hold to Copy (Unsafe)’ option. You can also always allow a website to copy things into your clipboard and you won’t get such a warning again for that site. Paste Protect combines Opera’s already existing Hijack protection feature with a new and unique Injection protection element. Hijack protection, which we introduced in 2021, protected your clipboard from hijack attempts – e.g. replacing a URL you copied with a different one that takes to a malicious site, or replacing a bank account number you’re trying to transfer to with a different one. Paste Protect is activated on your Opera browser by default. It can be turned on and off in the browser settings under the Paste Protect options. Get protected by downloading Opera Download Opera One here to get access to the Paste Protect feature. For more detailed information about this unique feature, remember to check the article we prepared about it here . Always remember to be cautious when it comes to copying and pasting commands, stay safe out there!

title: FAA Issues Heart Aerospace Special Airworthiness Certificate for X1 Demonstrator Aircraft
summary: The FAA has issued a Special Airworthiness Certificate for Heart Aerospace’s X1 demonstrator, authorizing flight testing to begin immediately.
body_text: PLATTSBURGH, NY, and LOS ANGELES, CA, July 23, 2026 – Heart Aerospace today announced that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a Special Airworthiness Certificate in the Experimental Category (SAC-EC) for its X1 demonstrator aircraft. The certificate authorizes Heart to commence flight testing of the X1 immediately. The FAA issued the certificate following an inspection of the aircraft at Heart’s X1 flight-test base at Plattsburgh International Airport in upstate New York, where the demonstrator is undergoing final preparations for its first flight. As part of its review, the agency evaluated the aircraft, supporting technical documentation, and Heart’s proposed flight-test operations. The certificate marks the culmination of more than a year of collaboration between Heart Aerospace and the FAA. Receipt of the SAC-EC follows Heart’s extensive X1 ground testing program, which included structural, propulsion, systems, and low- and high-speed taxi tests. Together, these activities demonstrated the aircraft’s readiness to proceed to piloted flight testing. “Earning FAA flight authorization brings the X1 program to the threshold of first flight,” said Anders Forslund, Founder and CEO of Heart Aerospace. “This achievement reflects the rigor of the work completed by Heart’s engineering and flight-test teams, as well as the close working relationship we have built with the FAA. With our certificate now in hand, our full focus is on flight. We are ready to get X1 in the air.” With a wingspan of 106 feet, a fuselage length of 76 feet, and a takeoff weight of more than 25,000 pounds, X1 is expected to be the largest electric aircraft ever flown. Developed as a full-scale demonstrator for Heart’s ES-30 production aircraft, a 30-seat hybrid-electric regional airliner, X1 will validate flight characteristics, demonstrate key technologies, and generate operational data and insights to support the ES-30’s continued development. “Heart is grateful to the FAA for its partnership,” said Cole Randle, Head of Corporate Affairs. “The agency’s forward-looking approach to next-generation aircraft is accelerating commercial aviation’s entry into the electric era of flight while supporting Heart’s mission to lower the cost of air travel. We look forward to continuing our work together as we pursue certification of the ES-30.” About Heart Aerospace Heart Aerospace is a Los Angeles-based electric aircraft manufacturer on a mission to lower the cost of air travel. The company's first production aircraft, the ES-30, is a clean-sheet, 30-seat hybrid-electric regional aircraft designed to bring cost-efficient electric flight into everyday airline service. Backed by a $9.4 billion order book from leading carriers including United Airlines and Air Canada, Heart is advancing the technologies to make electric aviation work at commercial scale. Learn more about Heart and its vision for abundant, affordable air travel at www.heartaerospace.com . Media Contact Cole Randle Head of Corporate Affairs press@heartaerospace.com +1-310-561-5193 # # #

title: [Public Alpha] Supabase Pipelines
summary: [Public Alpha] Supabase Pipelines
body_text: What's new # Supabase Pipelines is a managed change-data-capture service, powered by the open-source Supabase ETL engine, that streams changes from your Supabase Postgres database to external destinations in near real time. You pick a destination in the Dashboard, and Supabase runs and monitors the pipeline that keeps it in sync, reading directly from the Postgres write-ahead log. What you can do: Near real-time streaming — a complete initial copy of your selected tables, then near real-time replication of inserts, updates, deletes, and truncates, with at-least-once delivery. Granular control over what's replicated — publish specific tables, a whole schema, or all tables. Narrow to column subsets, filter rows with a WHERE clause, and handle partitioned tables. Automatic schema change support — supported changes (adding, removing, and renaming columns, and changing nullability and defaults) are detected and applied to the destination automatically. Full Dashboard management — create, start, stop, and restart pipelines, add or remove tables without restarting replication from scratch, and tune advanced settings like batch wait time, sync workers, and slot recovery. Monitoring — track pipeline status, metrics, and logs from the Dashboard. Reliable recovery — replication resumes from the last acknowledged position after a restart, detecting and recovering from many transient failures automatically while surfacing issues that require intervention. Workload isolation — replicate to an analytical destination so heavy queries run there, not on your production database. Destinations: BigQuery is the first destination available to everyone in public alpha. ClickHouse, Snowflake, and DuckLake are available on request through the early access form . Pricing during the public alpha: $0.053 per hour per active pipeline, $0.60/GB for the initial table copy, and $3/GB for replicated data after that. How to use it # Open the Dashboard and choose the tables to replicate. Pick a destination — BigQuery, at launch (or request ClickHouse, Snowflake, or DuckLake through the early access form ). Pipelines runs an initial copy of the selected tables, parallelized across and within tables for faster loading. After the copy completes, the pipeline switches to streaming mode. New changes are read from the replication slot, batched, and written to the destination. Supported schema changes are detected and applied to the destination automatically. Data is replicated as-is, without transformation. Why we built this # Postgres is excellent for transactional workloads: reading a user profile, inserting an order, updating a subscription, or serving your application. Analytics workloads are different. They often scan large amounts of data, aggregate across many rows, and power dashboards, reports, notebooks, and downstream systems. Running those queries directly on your production database can add load to the same system your application depends on. Supabase Pipelines gives you a reliable way to move production data into systems built for analytics, while keeping your application workload on Postgres.

title: Ally Financial declares dividend on common stock and Series C and Series D preferred stock
summary: The board of directors of Ally Financial Inc. (NYSE: ALLY) declared a quarterly cash dividend of $0.30 per share of the company's common stock, payable on August 14, 2026, to shareholders of...
body_text: DETROIT , July 20, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- The board of directors of Ally Financial Inc. (NYSE: ALLY) declared a quarterly cash dividend of $0.30 per share of the company's common stock, payable on August 14, 2026, to shareholders of record on July 31, 2026, as well as quarterly dividend payments for the company's Series C and Series D preferred stock securities, payable on August 15, 2026. A quarterly dividend payment was declared on Ally's 4.700% Fixed-Rate Reset Non-Cumulative Perpetual Preferred Stock, Series C, of approximately $11.8 million, or $11.75 per share, and is payable to shareholders of record as of July 31, 2026. Additionally, a dividend payment was declared on Ally's 7.100% Fixed-Rate Reset Non-Cumulative Perpetual Preferred Stock, Series D, of approximately $20.5 million, or $20.51 per share, and is payable to shareholders of record as of July 31, 2026. About Ally Financial Ally Financial Inc. (NYSE: ALLY) includes the nation's largest all-digital bank and auto finance business, driven by a mission to "Do It Right" for its customers and communities. Ally is a U.S. financial holding company with $197 billion in assets and 9.5 million customers (March 31, 2026). Ally Bank, Member FDIC, offers online banking products, including high-yield savings and no hidden fee checking, and was the first major U.S. bank to eliminate overdraft fees. Ally also provides investing solutions through Ally Invest, including online brokerage, automated investing, IRAs and personal advice. As a leader in auto finance, Ally provides consumer and dealer financing, insurance, and vehicle remarketing services. Ally's seasoned corporate finance business provides capital to equity sponsors and middle-market companies. Visit ally.com.
